In 1979 Mary Leakey announced the discovery at Laetoli in Tanzania of a 27 metre trail of hominin footprints preserved in volcanic ash dated to approximately 3.6 million years ago.
Switched the customer billing tables from Postgres 15 to CockroachDB v24 after the Frankfurt failover drill exposed a six-minute RPO gap with streaming replication.
Customer billing tables run on a three-region CockroachDB cluster spanning us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-2 with SERIALIZABLE isolation and survival goal region.
Chose Redis Enterprise with Active-Active CRDTs over a self-managed Redis Cluster because the ops team could not justify on-call rotation for gossip failures.
Session and rate-limit state lives in a five-shard Redis Enterprise database with Active-Active replication across two datacenters and 15 GB RAM per shard.
Adopted Kafka 3.7 with KRaft mode in place of RabbitMQ after the order-events topic backlog kept crashing the broker during Black Friday load tests.
The event backbone is a nine-broker Kafka 3.7 cluster in KRaft mode with a replication factor of three and tiered storage to S3 after seven days.
Picked Kong Gateway 3.6 over AWS API Gateway because the platform team needed declarative config in Git and sub-millisecond plugin latency at the edge.
Edge traffic terminates at a Kong Gateway 3.6 deployment of six pods behind an NLB, with rate-limit-advanced, OIDC, and request-transformer plugins applied per route.
Decided to replace the home-grown JWT issuer with Keycloak 24 after the third CVE in the custom token signer in nine months.
Authentication flows through a Keycloak 24 realm backed by a Postgres HA pair, issuing RS256 JWTs with a 15-minute access token and 30-day refresh token rotation.
Adopted Istio ambient mesh over the sidecar model because injecting Envoy into every pod doubled memory usage on the GPU inference nodes.
Cluster traffic runs on Istio 1.22 in ambient mode with ztunnel DaemonSets for L4 mTLS and per-namespace waypoint proxies handling L7 policy.
Switched from rolling updates to Argo Rollouts canary deployments after a bad image shipped to 60% of pods before the readiness probe caught it.
Production workloads deploy through Argo Rollouts with a 5/25/50/100 canary ladder gated on Prometheus latency and error SLO analyses between each step.
Chose OpenTelemetry Collector with the Tempo backend over Jaeger because we needed tail-based sampling and native OTLP receivers without a custom agent.
Tracing is collected by a three-tier OpenTelemetry Collector deployment (agent DaemonSet, load-balancing layer, tail-sampling gateway) feeding Grafana Tempo on S3.
Moved CI runners from hosted GitHub Actions to self-hosted Actions Runner Controller on EKS after monthly bills crossed thirty thousand dollars.
CI executes on an Actions Runner Controller deployment with ephemeral runners auto-scaling from 0 to 400 pods on Karpenter-provisioned spot instances.
Adopted Debezium on Kafka Connect over dual-writes after two customer-facing inconsistencies traced back to partial writes during deploys.
Change data capture runs through a Debezium 2.6 Kafka Connect cluster watching Postgres logical replication slots and fanning events into per-table topics.
Replaced Elasticsearch 7 with OpenSearch 2.13 after the license change and because kNN vector search on the product catalog needed faster iteration.
Product search runs on a three-master, twelve-data-node OpenSearch 2.13 cluster with a dedicated kNN index using HNSW and 768-dimensional embeddings.
Chose NVIDIA Triton Inference Server over a Flask wrapper after p99 latency on the recommender model doubled under concurrent tenants.
The recommender endpoint is served by Triton 24.05 running TensorRT engines on four A10G GPUs with dynamic batching up to 32 requests per 5 ms window.
Moved cold archives from EFS to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after storage costs exceeded the compute bill for the compliance pipeline.
Compliance artifacts older than 30 days live in an S3 bucket with an Intelligent-Tiering policy that demotes objects to Glacier Instant Retrieval at 90 days.
Standardized on Apache Parquet with Zstandard over CSV for analytics exports because query planners skipped 80% of row groups with column statistics.
Analytics exports land as Parquet files partitioned by event_date and tenant_id, compressed with Zstd level 3 and registered in the Glue Data Catalog.
Picked Centrifugo 5 over a custom Socket.IO service after the in-house fanout server dropped messages beyond 20 000 concurrent subscribers.
Realtime notifications flow through a Centrifugo 5 cluster of eight nodes joined by a Redis Streams engine, sustaining 120 000 concurrent WebSocket clients.
Adopted Neo4j 5 Aura over a homemade adjacency-list table when multi-hop fraud queries started timing out past three joins.
The fraud graph lives in a Neo4j 5 Aura Enterprise instance with a core of three and two read replicas, indexed on actor_id and device_fingerprint.
Switched from Airflow 2 to Temporal because long-running human-approval workflows kept expiring executor slots and wedging the scheduler.
Durable workflows run on a Temporal Cloud namespace with Go workers sharded by task queue and a 30-day workflow execution retention window.
Chose ClickHouse Cloud over Snowflake for product telemetry after the per-query costs on high-cardinality dashboards became unsustainable.
Product telemetry is stored in a ClickHouse Cloud service with a ReplicatedMergeTree engine partitioned by toYYYYMM(event_time) and a 180-day TTL.
Migrated from Docker Engine to containerd on all Kubernetes nodes after dockershim removal in Kubernetes 1.24 and to drop an unnecessary daemon.
All Kubernetes nodes run containerd 1.7 as the CRI runtime with the systemd cgroup driver and nerdctl available for debug shells on the host.
Adopted HashiCorp Vault over AWS Secrets Manager when multi-cloud GCP workloads needed the same dynamic database credentials flow.
Secrets live in a Vault Enterprise cluster of five Raft nodes with the database and transit engines enabled and auto-unseal via AWS KMS.
Picked Qdrant over pgvector for the code-assistant embeddings after recall dropped below 0.85 at 40 million vectors on a shared Postgres instance.
Code embeddings are stored in a Qdrant 1.9 cluster of six shards with HNSW indexes (m=32, ef_construct=256) and payload-based tenant filtering.
Adopted LiteLLM Proxy in front of OpenAI and Anthropic after prompt-injection logging and per-team spend caps could not be enforced at the SDK layer.
All LLM calls from IDE plugins route through a LiteLLM Proxy deployment with Redis for rate-limit state, Postgres for virtual-key budgets, and Langfuse for traces.
Chose Anthropic prompt caching for the repo-context block after measuring a 9x latency improvement on follow-up messages that re-send the same system prompt.
The code-assistant system prompt and repo manifest are sent as two cache_control=ephemeral blocks so the 30 000-token prefix is reused for five minutes across turns.
Added a Cohere Rerank 3 stage after BM25 because top-1 accuracy on StackOverflow-style queries sat at 54% without cross-encoder scoring.
Retrieval runs a hybrid pipeline: BM25 over Tantivy plus dense search over Qdrant, fused by RRF, then the top 40 hits are reranked by Cohere Rerank 3 before prompt assembly.
Chose tree-sitter over LSP for symbol extraction because the indexer had to work on partial files checked out from commits without a running language server.
The code indexer parses each file with tree-sitter grammars for Python, TypeScript, Go, and Rust, emitting a unified symbol table with byte-offset ranges into pgvector chunks.
Adopted a dual-store memory (mem0 plus memora) because pure semantic recall kept missing structured items like ticket IDs and assignees.
Agent memory is split across mem0 for natural-language facts and memora for tag-indexed structured entries, queried in parallel on every user turn.
Switched the code embedder from text-embedding-3-large to bge-code-v1 after internal evals showed a 6-point nDCG gain on cross-repo queries and 10x lower cost.
Code chunks are embedded by a self-hosted bge-code-v1 model on two L4 GPUs behind vLLM, producing 1024-dimensional vectors ingested into Qdrant.
Chose JSON Schema tool definitions with strict mode over free-form function calls after 4% of agent outputs produced unparsable arguments under load.
Tool calls are defined as Anthropic tools with strict JSON Schema input definitions validated by pydantic on the server before dispatch to the handler registry.
Adopted Promptfoo for offline regression runs because ad-hoc Jupyter evaluations made diffs between prompt versions impossible to review.
Prompt changes trigger a Promptfoo CI job that runs 400 fixture prompts against the new and old prompt variants and publishes a diff report to the PR.
Chose Gitleaks in a pre-receive hook over a nightly scan after a leaked API token made it into main and took six hours to notice.
The Git server enforces a Gitleaks pre-receive hook with a custom rule set and quarantine pushed refs until the scan exits cleanly.
Adopted OpenFeature with a flagd provider over LaunchDarkly for non-customer-facing flags because the team wanted on-cluster evaluation and no egress.
Feature flags are served by flagd sidecars per pod reading a Git-synced ConfigMap, with SDKs talking localhost:8013 via the OpenFeature SDK.
Chose self-hosted Sentry over the SaaS offering after data-residency requirements from the EU customer demanded no telemetry leaving Frankfurt.
Exceptions are captured by a self-hosted Sentry 24 deployment on eu-central-1 with ClickHouse for events and an 11-day retention per project.
Picked Vector over Fluent Bit for log shipping after the memory footprint under 30k events/s made Fluent Bit OOM on the smaller nodes.
Logs flow from each node via a Vector DaemonSet through a Kafka transform topic and into Loki, with a parallel sink to S3 for long-term archival.
Moved from standalone Prometheus to Mimir after cardinality from per-user labels pushed the single instance past 50 GB of head series.
Metrics are written by Prometheus agents remote-writing to a Grafana Mimir cluster with four ingesters, three store-gateways, and S3 long-term blocks storage.
Adopted Okta for workforce SSO because the previous Google Workspace-only setup could not integrate with the new SOC 2 session policies.
All internal tools authenticate via Okta SAML with a 12-hour session, device-trust verification, and SCIM provisioning into the employee directory.
Chose NS1 managed DNS over Route 53 because latency-based steering across multiple cloud providers required per-answer filter chains.
External DNS is hosted on NS1 with filter-chain records performing geo, latency, and up/down health checks across AWS, GCP, and on-prem origins.
Adopted Fastly in front of S3 because the product team needed edge compute with VCL to handle signed-URL rewrites closer to the user.
Static assets and media segments are served via Fastly with a custom VCL service that validates short-lived HMAC tokens before hitting origin S3 buckets.
Switched the monorepo from Lerna to Turborepo 2 after build times on a twelve-package workspace exceeded twenty minutes on developer laptops.
The TypeScript monorepo is orchestrated by Turborepo 2 with a remote cache hosted on Vercel, task graph derived from package.json, and pnpm workspaces underneath.
Chose Vitest over Jest for the darkraise-ui package after ESM support and Vite HMR made the prior Jest setup impossible to maintain.
Frontend unit tests run under Vitest 1.6 with happy-dom, parallelized across eight workers and reporting coverage via v8 into a JUnit XML for CI.
Adopted Ruff over Flake8 and isort because running three tools on every commit doubled pre-commit latency and caused developers to skip hooks.
Python linting runs a single Ruff 0.5 invocation configured in pyproject.toml with E, F, I, UP, and B rule sets and an auto-fix stage in the pre-commit hook.
Switched from pip-tools to uv after lockfile resolution on the backend service dropped from 90 seconds to under three.
Python environments are managed with uv 0.4, using a pyproject.toml plus uv.lock checked into git and an in-CI uv sync --frozen to install deterministic dependencies.
Chose Harbor over Docker Hub Enterprise for internal images because CVE scanning and project-level RBAC were both required for the FedRAMP audit.
Internal container images live in a Harbor 2.10 registry with Trivy scanning, Notary signing, and replication to a warm standby registry in a second region.
Adopted Consul over Kubernetes Services because bare-metal VMs outside the cluster still had to participate in the same service catalog.
Service discovery is centralized in a Consul cluster of five servers with Consul agents on every VM and Kubernetes pod, exposing DNS on the local node at 127.0.0.1:8600.
Picked Terraform Enterprise over Pulumi because the platform team had ten years of HCL modules that could not realistically be rewritten.
Infrastructure is codified in Terraform 1.8 modules stored in a central repository, executed by Terraform Enterprise workspaces with Sentinel policies and Vault-issued cloud credentials.
Adopted Changesets for versioning because manual npm publish commits kept going out of sync across the five public packages in the repo.
The monorepo publishes packages via Changesets with a GitHub Action that opens a Version Packages PR, then runs changeset publish to npm on merge to main.
Chose Alembic with a single-head policy over bespoke SQL files after a merge produced two concurrent head revisions that broke production on deploy.
Database migrations are versioned with Alembic, enforced single-head by a CI check, and applied during a dedicated pre-deploy Kubernetes Job before rollout.
Adopted SLSA level 3 provenance on all release binaries after a supply-chain tabletop exercise revealed no way to verify which commit produced a given image.
Release pipelines emit SLSA v1.0 provenance attestations signed by Sigstore cosign and stored alongside images in the OCI registry under the .att tag.
Chose Cloudflare Workers over AWS Lambda for the URL-shortener edge tier because cold starts dominated p95 latency at 400 ms on Lambda.
The URL-shortener runs as a Cloudflare Worker deployed to the global network with Workers KV for hot lookups and a D1 database as the durable store.
Adopted TimescaleDB over vanilla Postgres for IoT telemetry after ingest past 40k rows/second caused lock contention on the btree indexes.
IoT telemetry is written to a TimescaleDB 2.15 hypertable chunked by one-hour intervals with continuous aggregates refreshed every five minutes for dashboard queries.
Picked Avro with a Confluent Schema Registry over raw JSON on Kafka after two consumer teams silently diverged on the order-created payload.
Kafka topics carry Avro-encoded messages validated against a Confluent Schema Registry with BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE compatibility and subject naming of <topic>-value.
Moved to trunk-based development after two long feature branches collided during a release freeze.
All engineers commit to main behind feature flags; short-lived branches merge within 24 hours and the release is cut from main every Thursday.
We chose mandatory two-reviewer approval after a silent auth regression slipped through a single-approver merge last quarter.
Pull requests require two human approvals plus a green CI run before the merge queue will accept them; the CODEOWNERS file routes security-sensitive paths to the platform team.
We adopted a merge queue because concurrent PR merges kept breaking main two or three times per week.
GitHub's merge queue serialises integration: each PR is rebased onto the tip, re-runs the full test matrix, and only lands if the pipeline stays green for the whole sequence.
We moved from biweekly trains to daily releases once the smoke-test pipeline dropped below ten minutes.

Every green build on main promotes to staging at 10:00 UTC and to production at 15:00 UTC on business days, gated by an automated canary analysis that watches error rate and latency for fifteen minutes.
We adopted a commander-plus-scribe-plus-comms role split after our first SEV1 lasted four hours because nobody was driving.

Every SEV1 page opens a dedicated Slack channel, assigns an incident commander, a scribe, and a communications lead; the commander owns technical decisions while the scribe keeps a running timeline for the postmortem.
We chose a follow-the-sun rotation because the EU on-call was paging at 3 AM twice a week.

Three regional rotations cover US-West, EU, and APAC in eight-hour windows; the primary on-call owns acknowledgement within five minutes and handoffs happen in a shared channel with an explicit written summary of open incidents.
We dropped two-week sprints in favour of continuous flow after retros kept surfacing the same end-of-sprint crunch.

Work is tracked on a single pull-based board with explicit work-in-progress limits per column; weekly demos replace sprint reviews and planning happens as a thirty-minute backlog refinement each Monday.
We adopted CODEOWNERS-enforced ownership after an orphaned service caused a seven-hour outage with no clear responder.
Every top-level directory maps to exactly one owning team in CODEOWNERS; ownership changes require a signed ADR and the platform team audits the mapping quarterly against the service catalog.
We introduced a lightweight RFC process after three teams independently built their own feature-flag systems in the same quarter.

Any change with cross-team impact lands as a markdown RFC in the architecture repo, collects comments for five business days, and is ratified by the principal engineers' group before implementation begins.
We switched to blameless postmortems after engineers started hiding near-misses to avoid being named in the writeups.

Every SEV2-and-above incident gets a written postmortem within five business days; the document focuses on contributing factors and systemic fixes, names no individuals as at fault, and its action items are tracked to completion in the issue tracker.
We moved to structured interviews with calibrated rubrics after a hiring manager audit showed wildly different bars across loops.

Every candidate goes through the same four stages: recruiter screen, a coding exercise, a system-design round, and a values interview; each stage has a written rubric and two interviewers must independently submit scores before the debrief.
We chose a buddy-plus-checklist onboarding model after new hires reported feeling lost for their entire first month.

Each new engineer is paired with a buddy for thirty days, works through a written onboarding checklist covering environment setup, first PR, first on-call shadow, and first incident readout, and checks in weekly with their manager against that list.
We set a four-hour review SLA after throughput data showed PRs sitting unreviewed for a median of two business days.
Pull requests awaiting review ping the owning team's channel after four business hours and escalate to the team lead after eight; a weekly dashboard tracks the median time-in-review per team.
We adopted a Friday and holiday-eve deploy freeze after three Friday deploys turned into weekend incidents.

Production deploys are blocked from Friday 14:00 UTC through Monday 09:00 UTC and for twenty-four hours before recognised holidays; exceptions require the on-call director's written approval in the deploy channel.
We made rollback the default response for production SEV1s after a forward-fix attempt doubled the length of the outage.

Any SEV1 that correlates with a recent deploy triggers an automatic rollback within ten minutes unless the incident commander explicitly opts for a forward-fix and documents the reason in the channel.
We introduced a flag-expiry policy after discovering more than two hundred stale flags that nobody remembered owning.

Every new feature flag is created with an owner and an expiry date; a weekly job opens a tracking ticket for any flag past its expiry and flags more than ninety days old fail the release readiness check.
We adopted an error-budget-based freeze rule after the reliability team and product kept arguing about when to slow feature work.
Each service has a monthly error budget derived from its SLO; once the budget is exhausted feature deploys are automatically blocked and only reliability fixes ship until the rolling window recovers.
We made threat modelling a required gate after a high-severity data-exposure bug shipped without any security sign-off.

Features touching authentication, authorization, or PII require a written threat model reviewed by the security team before implementation begins; the review is linked from the RFC and tracked on the release checklist.
We started requiring pairing on critical-path changes after a solo refactor of the payments module caused a two-hour incident.
Any change to code paths tagged critical in the service catalog is authored in a pairing session; the pairing partner co-signs the PR and the session is noted in the commit trailer.
We moved retros from ad-hoc to biweekly after three months of retros happening only when something went wrong.

Each squad runs a sixty-minute retrospective every second Friday using a start-stop-continue template; action items are captured in the team board and the squad lead reviews progress against them at the next retro.
We shifted from annual to semi-annual performance reviews after engineers said yearly feedback came too late to act on.

Performance reviews run every six months on a fixed calendar; each review combines manager assessment, peer feedback from three nominated colleagues, and a self-reflection, all captured in the HR system for continuity.
We adopted an inner-source model after platform teams became a bottleneck for every cross-team feature request.

Shared infrastructure repositories accept pull requests from any engineer in the company; each repo has a published contributing guide, a maintainer rotation, and an SLA for first response on outside contributions.
We made design review mandatory for all services with customer-facing APIs after two teams shipped incompatible webhook shapes.

Any service exposing an external API runs a design review with the API council before the first endpoint ships; the council checks naming, versioning, error shape, and rate-limit defaults against the company API guidelines.
We moved to expand-contract migrations after a destructive alter-table locked the orders database for twenty minutes.

Schema changes ship in two deploys: the first adds the new shape and dual-writes, the second removes the old shape after a verified backfill; destructive statements run only behind a feature flag and a documented rollback script.
We adopted a monthly dependency upgrade train after a six-month-stale library left us exposed to a published CVE.

A scheduled job opens upgrade PRs the first Monday of each month for every direct dependency; the platform team triages and merges them by the end of that week, and any unmerged upgrades roll into the next month's review.
We made docs a release-blocker after an incident revealed the runbook for a tier-one service hadn't been updated in a year.

Each service has a runbook and an architecture page owned by the same team that owns the code; a CI check fails the deploy if either page has not been touched in the last ninety days and the service had a code change in that window.
We formalised escalation levels after an on-call engineer struggled alone on a customer-visible outage for ninety minutes.

Every SEV1 escalates to the secondary on-call after ten minutes without acknowledgement, to the engineering manager after thirty, and to the director after sixty; the escalation path is encoded in the pager policy and tested monthly via game days.
We adopted a weekly bug bash plus a rotating triage role after the backlog crossed one thousand open issues.

A triage engineer rotates weekly across the squad and owns all incoming bugs: every new issue is labelled, severity-scored, and either routed to a milestone or closed within two business days, and the team spends Friday afternoons on a themed bug bash.
We introduced a weekly experiment council after three A/B tests shipped with overlapping audiences and unreadable results.

Every experiment is registered in the experiment platform before launch and reviewed in a Tuesday council meeting; the council checks audience overlap, power analysis, and stopping criteria, and signs off before the flag is turned on.
We chose Black plus Ruff on autoformat after a style debate dominated three consecutive engineering all-hands.

Every Python repository runs Black and Ruff in a pre-commit hook and in CI; style discussions in PRs are closed by pointing at the configured tooling and any rule change requires a one-line RFC in the style repo.
We set a coverage floor on changed lines only after a blanket eighty-percent rule pushed teams to write useless tests.

The CI check enforces that at least seventy-five percent of lines changed in a PR are exercised by tests; whole-file coverage is reported as a trend but does not block merges, keeping the incentive on testing new work.
We separated security incidents from reliability incidents after a credential leak got lost in the general ops channel.

Security incidents follow a distinct runbook and page the security team first; the response channel is access-controlled, evidence is preserved in a dedicated bucket, and legal is looped in within the first hour for any data-exposure class.
We made accessibility review a launch gate for customer-facing UI after an external audit found WCAG violations on the checkout flow.
Every customer-visible UI change is reviewed against the WCAG 2.2 AA checklist by the accessibility guild before launch; automated axe-core tests run in CI and block merges on new violations.
We chose to buy rather than build for observability tooling after the internal metrics stack consumed half of an SRE team for a year.

Observability runs on a vendor platform with a clear integration layer; the SRE team owns the integration and dashboards while product engineers consume the tooling through a thin internal SDK, freeing the team to focus on reliability work.
We moved to ephemeral preview environments after a shared staging cluster became the bottleneck for every large feature.

Each PR spins up its own namespaced environment on the dev cluster with seeded data; the environment is torn down automatically when the PR merges or after forty-eight hours of inactivity, and a shared long-lived staging is reserved for end-to-end regression tests.
We adopted a written kickoff doc for every epic after multiple features shipped without clear success criteria.

Each epic begins with a one-page kickoff doc covering problem statement, success metrics, non-goals, and rollout plan; engineering manager, product manager, and tech lead all sign off before the first ticket is opened.
We reserved twenty percent of each quarter for tech-debt work after two years of debt tickets never making it into sprints.

Each team's quarterly plan allocates a dedicated debt bucket equal to one in five engineer-weeks; debt items are prioritised by the tech lead and reported alongside feature progress in the quarterly business review.
We locked down production shell access after an accidental rm on a live host caused a two-hour data recovery effort.

Direct shell access to production hosts is disabled; engineers use an audited break-glass tool that opens a time-boxed session, records every command, and requires a peer's approval before granting elevated privileges.
We introduced a formal vendor review after a shadow-IT SaaS purchase exposed customer data to an unvetted processor.

Any new third-party service that touches customer or production data goes through a joint security, legal, and procurement review; approved vendors are listed in a shared registry and renewals trigger an automatic re-review.
We adopted quarterly OKRs after yearly goal-setting kept drifting out of relevance by the third month.

Each team sets three to five objectives with measurable key results at the start of every quarter; progress is reviewed at a mid-quarter checkpoint and scored publicly at the end, and the results feed into the next quarter's planning.
We replaced change advisory board approval with automated release readiness checks after CAB meetings added a day of latency with no measurable safety gain.

Releases are approved by an automated readiness pipeline that verifies green tests, a signed-off runbook entry, an up-to-date rollback script, and the absence of active incidents; exceptions still require a director's written approval.
We committed to writing ADRs for every significant choice after an architecture quiz showed half the team could not explain why we picked Kafka.

Architecture decisions land as numbered ADRs in the docs repo using the context-decision-consequences template; every PR that introduces a new service or replaces an existing one must link to the relevant ADR, and the index is reviewed at the quarterly architecture summit.
We introduced a weekly Friday demo after stakeholders complained they only saw finished work at quarter boundaries.

Every Friday at 16:00 local, each squad shows a fifteen-minute demo of shipped or shippable work; recordings go to a shared Drive folder and the engineering newsletter links the week's highlights for asynchronous viewers.
We adopted a monthly game day after a region-failover drill revealed nobody had actually tested the DNS switch under load.

Each month one squad runs a pre-announced game day that injects a realistic failure mode in staging and, quarterly, in production under a tight blast radius; findings are tracked as normal incidents with owned remediation items.
We introduced a runbook drill after an on-call engineer couldn't follow an outdated Redis failover doc during a real page.

Each tier-one service's runbook is exercised by its on-call once per quarter in a staging drill; any step that doesn't work is fixed inside the drill window and the runbook's last-verified date is stamped at the top of the page.
We committed to upstreaming internal patches after maintaining a private fork of a key library consumed weeks of engineer time every upgrade.

Every internal patch to an external dependency is opened as a pull request upstream within two weeks; until it lands we track the fork in a shared board and the platform team owns keeping the fork rebased against the upstream main branch.
We started a biweekly engineering talk after survey feedback flagged lack of cross-team technical visibility.

A thirty-minute engineering talk runs every other Wednesday with a rotating speaker drawn from the signup sheet; talks are recorded, slides are archived in the learning repo, and attendance is optional but counted towards the growth rubric.
We adopted a shared experiment log after three teams re-ran the same onboarding experiment unaware of each other's results.

Every experiment writes an entry in the company-wide experiment log with hypothesis, setup, result, and decision; the log is searchable by feature area and new experiment proposals must check for prior art before approval.
We moved promotions to a calibrated committee review after manager-only promotions produced noticeable inconsistencies between teams.

Promotion packets are written against a public rubric by the candidate's manager, reviewed by a cross-team committee that calibrates against anonymised past packets, and decided in a single meeting that produces a written rationale for each outcome.
We dropped formal change approval forms in favour of a lightweight change log after the forms became copy-paste rituals everyone ignored.

Every production-impacting change posts a structured message in the change channel with author, scope, rollback plan, and monitoring link; the log is archived for audit and reviewed in the weekly reliability meeting for patterns.
Moved from self-managed Kubernetes to GKE Autopilot after the fourth CVE scramble in a quarter cost us two weekends.
Workloads run on a GKE Autopilot cluster in europe-west1 fronted by a global HTTPS load balancer with Cloud Armor WAF rules.
Chose AKS over EKS for the new Azure commitment; the existing Enterprise Agreement absorbed the control plane cost entirely.
The staging cluster is an AKS deployment in westeurope with three node pools: system, general workloads, and GPU-tainted inference nodes.
Swapped Calico for Cilium after the eBPF datapath benchmarks showed 30 percent lower p99 latency on east-west traffic.
Pod networking runs on Cilium in kube-proxy-replacement mode with Hubble exporting flow logs to the observability cluster.
Decided to keep Route 53 for public zones and CoreDNS for cluster-internal resolution instead of unifying on one provider.
Public records live in Route 53 with health-checked failover while in-cluster lookups resolve via CoreDNS with a stub zone for corp.internal.
Moved gRPC ingress off ALBs onto NLBs after HTTP/2 connection reuse repeatedly pinned pods on a single target for minutes.
gRPC traffic terminates on an NLB in each region which forwards to Envoy ingress pods that handle TLS and per-method routing.
Chose Cloudflare over Fastly for the CDN layer because bundled bot management and WAF were a single contract.
Static assets and image origin are fronted by Cloudflare CDN with cache-key normalisation and a same-origin worker injecting CSP headers.
Dropped the Docker shim on worker nodes in favour of containerd after Kubernetes 1.24 made the deprecation final.
All nodes run containerd 1.7 with the systemd cgroup driver; image pulling goes through a Harbor mirror on the same subnet.
Migrated the colo hypervisors from VMware vSphere to Proxmox VE once the Broadcom licensing hike made renewal untenable.
The colo runs two Proxmox VE clusters of four nodes each with Ceph RBD as the shared storage backend for live migration.
Replaced the CloudFormation stacks with Terraform so we could manage AWS, GCP, and Cloudflare from one tool and one state backend.
Infrastructure is defined in Terraform with state stored in an S3 bucket plus DynamoDB locks, organised into per-environment workspaces.
Picked Pulumi with TypeScript over another Terraform rollout because the platform team wanted real types and unit tests on stack outputs.
The platform code is a Pulumi TypeScript monorepo that exposes a handful of component resources wrapping AWS, GitHub, and Datadog providers.
Retired the self-hosted HashiCorp Vault cluster in favour of AWS Secrets Manager; the ops cost of two Vault outages per quarter was not worth it.
Application secrets sit in AWS Secrets Manager with rotation lambdas on a 30-day cadence and IAM-scoped access per service role.
Standardised on SOPS with age keys for all in-repo secrets instead of encrypted dotenv files scattered per service.
Each repo ships a .sops.yaml declaring its age recipients and a CI job decrypts the selected file into a short-lived env at deploy time.
Moved away from the internal CA-signed certificates to ACME via Let's Encrypt after the internal CA expired unnoticed and took two regions offline.
All ingress certificates are issued by cert-manager through the Let's Encrypt production issuer with HTTP-01 challenges terminated at the edge.
Kept the private PKI for workload mTLS even after moving public edges to ACME; service identity belongs to us, not a public CA.
Workload identities are issued by an internal SPIFFE-compatible CA with 24-hour certificates distributed by a sidecar on every pod.
Adopted pgBackRest for Postgres backups after pg_dump slots held the WAL for hours and pushed disks to 95 percent on the primary.
Each Postgres primary streams WAL to pgBackRest which writes full and differential backups to object storage with a 30-day retention window.
Decided Velero was mandatory before we let product teams run Argo apps with stateful charts in the shared cluster.
Velero runs on every cluster with a daily schedule that snapshots all namespaces and ships restic payloads plus PV snapshots to a regional bucket.
Rejected a cold DR target in favour of a warm standby after tabletop exercises showed we could not meet the 1-hour RTO with a cold spin-up.
DR lives in us-east-2 as a warm standby: Aurora global database replica, scaled-to-one Kubernetes deployments, and DNS weighted at 0 until failover.
Committed to active/active across two AWS regions instead of active/passive so the quarterly failover game days were no longer a fire drill.
Traffic is split 50/50 between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 via Route 53 latency records with per-region Aurora writers and conflict-free replicated state.
Dropped Datadog after the annual bill crossed mid six figures and the platform team said they could run the OSS stack for a fraction of the cost.
Observability runs on a self-hosted stack of Prometheus, Loki, Tempo, and Grafana with Mimir fronting long-term metric storage on S3.
Picked Honeycomb for production tracing over an internal Jaeger build; BubbleUp paid for itself in the first two incidents.
Application services emit OTLP spans to a Honeycomb ingest endpoint through a regional collector that handles sampling and tail-based retention.
Replaced the Fluentd daemonsets with Fluent Bit after the Ruby footprint cost us 1 GB of RAM per node for no functional gain.
Every node runs a Fluent Bit daemonset that tails container logs, enriches with Kubernetes metadata, and forwards to Loki over gRPC.
Chose Vector as the aggregation layer instead of Logstash because the config is typed and the pipeline can be unit-tested offline.
Per-region Vector aggregators receive logs from edge collectors, apply VRL-based PII scrubbing, and fan out to Loki, S3, and SIEM sinks.
Switched long-term metrics from Thanos to VictoriaMetrics; Thanos store-gateway cost and query latency at our cardinality were unworkable.
Metrics are scraped by vmagent, shipped to a vmcluster of three vmstorage nodes per region, and queried through vmselect behind Grafana.
Kept Prometheus at the cluster edge but remote-wrote everything into Mimir so the on-call teams never had to federate by hand again.
Each cluster runs a Prometheus pair with remote_write pointed at a central Mimir deployment backed by S3 for long-term blocks.
Standardised on the OpenTelemetry Collector as the single tracing ingress instead of running vendor agents next to each application.
Applications emit OTLP to a collector daemonset which batches, samples, and exports to Tempo for trace storage and to Mimir for RED metrics.
Cut Jaeger retention from 14 days to 3 after storage costs doubled in a quarter and nobody queried traces older than 48 hours.
Jaeger runs with a Cassandra backend limited to 3-day TTL per span index and an archive path for flagged traces that writes to S3 for 90 days.
Retired the hand-rolled WireGuard mesh in favour of Tailscale once the ACL tooling started reviewing itself and the key distribution broke in DR.
Operator access to prod flows through Tailscale with ACLs generated from the HR system and exit nodes landing in each cloud VPC.
Kept IPsec tunnels for partner B2B links even after migrating staff to Tailscale; partners require dedicated static-routed endpoints.
Partner integrations terminate on two IPsec VPN gateways in us-east-1 with BGP peering into a dedicated transit VPC that hosts the exchange services.
Killed the SSH bastion fleet and switched to AWS Session Manager; key rotation and just-in-time access were both solved for free.
Shell access to EC2 instances goes through AWS Session Manager with IAM roles gating which principals can start sessions on which tags.
Chose Teleport over Boundary for privileged access because the recording and RBAC model lined up cleanly with the SOC 2 audit requirements.
Teleport proxies sit in a dedicated VPC and broker SSH, Kubernetes, and Postgres sessions with full session recording to an S3 bucket.
Automated the regional failover runbook after the manual procedure missed a single Terraform variable and cost us another 20 minutes.
Failover is driven by a Step Functions state machine that flips Route 53 weights, promotes the Aurora replica, and drains the stale ASG in parallel.
Held the line on EU-only data storage for EU customers instead of a cheaper single-region design once GDPR legal review flagged the transfer risk.
EU customer data lives in two eu-west subnets with replicated Postgres and S3 buckets, all KMS-encrypted with keys that never leave the region.
Committed to a three-year compute Savings Plan covering 70 percent of baseline EC2 usage; the finance team signed off after the first quarterly review.
Baseline compute runs on reserved capacity backed by a compute Savings Plan with bursts served by on-demand and interruptible spot capacity.
Moved the batch ML fleet to spot-first after a month of checkpointing work proved interruptions were cheaper than on-demand pricing.
Batch training jobs run on a Karpenter-managed spot node group with per-job checkpointing to S3 and a fallback on-demand pool for stragglers.
Rolled the fleet from gp2 to gp3 volumes once the IOPS-per-dollar math became unambiguous at any volume size above 100 GiB.
All stateful workloads use gp3 volumes with baseline IOPS provisioned per workload tier and snapshot schedules managed by AWS Backup.
Stood up MinIO on the colo hardware instead of a pure cloud object store because the data residency contract required on-site copies.
On-prem object storage is a four-node MinIO cluster in erasure-coded mode behind an HAProxy layer with replication to an offsite S3 bucket.
Ripped out Istio after the third control-plane upgrade broke mTLS on a Friday afternoon; Linkerd's smaller surface area was worth the feature loss.
Service-to-service traffic flows through a Linkerd mesh with automatic mTLS and per-deployment traffic shift manifests driving progressive rollouts.
Chose Consul Connect over a pure Kubernetes mesh because half the workloads still run on VMs and needed the same identity fabric.
VMs and pods share identity through Consul Connect; envoy sidecars are injected by Nomad or the Kubernetes webhook depending on workload type.
Replaced the nginx ingress controller with Envoy-based Contour after per-tenant rate limiting turned into a lua maintenance problem.
Edge ingress runs Contour with Envoy data planes; per-tenant RateLimitPolicy CRDs feed into a global ratelimit service backed by Redis.
Consolidated three separate API gateways onto a single Kong deployment after plugin drift caused contradictory auth behaviours across teams.
All north-south HTTP traffic enters a Kong gateway tier where JWT validation, mTLS enforcement, and request transformation plugins run in a fixed order.
Moved the primary transactional database from self-managed Postgres on EC2 to Aurora PostgreSQL after the on-call rota blamed failovers three quarters running.
OLTP workloads run on an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with one writer and three readers, snapshotted daily and replicated to a second region for DR.
Chose CockroachDB Dedicated over self-hosting the same binary; we wanted the distributed SQL guarantees without owning the node repair story.
Ledger workloads run on CockroachDB Dedicated in a three-region configuration with survival mode set to region failure and backups to object storage.
Rejected a managed Redis in favour of self-hosted Redis Cluster once the managed per-shard pricing crossed the break-even against a small SRE rota.
The shared cache tier is a six-shard Redis Cluster on dedicated nodes with TLS between primaries and replicas and Sentinel wired only for failover detection.
Kept Memcached for session storage even after moving everything else to Redis; the single-purpose simplicity kept paging incidents at zero for two years.
Session data sits in a three-node Memcached fleet behind a consistent-hash client library with a TTL equal to the session cookie lifetime.
Retired the self-hosted RabbitMQ cluster in favour of SQS for general async work; quorum queue operations were eating one engineer-week per month.
Async jobs flow through SQS standard queues with a separate FIFO queue for billing writes and DLQs configured for five retries before alerting.
Stuck with self-managed Kafka rather than Kinesis because exactly-once semantics with compacted topics were not achievable on the managed offering when we evaluated.
Event backbone is a Kafka cluster of nine brokers per region using KRaft mode, TLS/SASL auth, and MirrorMaker 2 for cross-region topic replication.
Moved long CI pipelines from GitHub-hosted Actions to self-hosted Buildkite agents after single-job times consistently crossed the 6-hour hard limit.
CI runs on a Buildkite agent fleet autoscaled on EKS with ephemeral runners per job and a shared S3-backed artifact cache keyed by dependency lockfile hashes.
Adopted ArgoCD with Argo Rollouts over the home-grown deploy script once a bad canary slipped through and took 25 percent of traffic for 9 minutes.
Every service deploys via ArgoCD with Rollouts CRDs driving 5/25/50/100 percent canary steps gated on Prometheus analysis queries and manual approval at 50.
Shifted bot mitigation from an in-cluster nginx module up to Cloud Armor after a volumetric attack saturated the ingress NLB for 12 minutes.
Public traffic passes a Cloud Armor policy with managed bot rules, a rate-limit rule per origin IP, and a WAF preconfigured rule set for OWASP top 10.
Dropped symptom-based CPU alerts in favour of SLO-driven alerting because two years of page data showed CPU alerts had a 6 percent precision rate.
Alerting is driven by Sloth-generated SLOs; burn-rate alerts at 2 percent and 5 percent of the monthly budget page the on-call, everything else is a ticket.
Switched the event pipeline from Kinesis to Redpanda after throughput stopped keeping up with the dashboards.
Events land in a Redpanda topic, feed a Flink job, and materialise into Iceberg tables partitioned by event_date.
Moved the real-time aggregations off Spark Structured Streaming onto Flink once watermark handling became too brittle.
Flink jobs consume from Kafka, keyed by tenant_id, and sink rolling aggregates into a RocksDB-backed state store before emitting to a ClickHouse view.
Replaced the hand-written Airflow Bash tasks with dbt models so analytics engineers could own transformation logic.
dbt runs on a Snowflake warehouse, orchestrated by Airflow's KubernetesPodOperator, with sources mapped to raw Fivetran schemas.
Adopted Apache Iceberg over plain Parquet directories because partition evolution kept breaking our backfills.
Raw Parquet writes land in S3, a Glue job registers them as Iceberg tables, and Trino reads snapshots for ad-hoc analytics.
Chose BigQuery over Redshift for the new analytics surface since the workload was bursty and columnar scan costs dominated.
Fivetran lands CRM data into BigQuery raw datasets, dbt materialises marts, and Looker reads from a dedicated semantic layer project.
Migrated orchestration from Airflow to Dagster after asset-centric lineage became a hard requirement for the platform team.
Dagster assets define the warehouse graph, sensors poll S3 prefixes, and the daemon schedules partitioned backfills against the Snowflake target.
Picked Hightouch for reverse ETL so that go-to-market syncs stopped living in a brittle Python cron job.
Hightouch reads curated marts from Snowflake and syncs them into Salesforce and HubSpot on a 15-minute cadence with diff-based upserts.
Replaced the Kafka Connect JDBC source with Debezium for Postgres CDC because logical replication slots gave us ordered change streams.
Debezium reads from Postgres replication slots, publishes to Kafka topics per table, and a Flink job upserts them into an Iceberg mirror.
Introduced Confluent Schema Registry after a malformed Avro message silently corrupted a downstream mart for two days.
Producers register Avro schemas against the registry, Kafka brokers enforce compatibility, and consumers resolve schema ids lazily via a local cache.
Adopted Monte Carlo for data observability since our custom freshness checks could not cover cross-schema volume anomalies.
Monte Carlo agents query Snowflake INFORMATION_SCHEMA, detect freshness and volume anomalies, and post incidents into a dedicated Slack channel.
Standardised on Great Expectations over the bespoke assertion library because suites needed to be generated from JSON schemas.
Great Expectations runs inside Airflow, validates Parquet batches on S3, and writes data docs back to a versioned S3 bucket.
Chose OpenLineage over the hand-maintained lineage wiki so upstream breakages would show up in pager alerts.
Airflow emits OpenLineage events to a Marquez backend, dbt runs feed run-level lineage, and the UI surfaces downstream impact graphs.
Moved PII tokenisation from an in-app library to Skyflow after auditors flagged inconsistent masking across services.
Skyflow stores raw PII behind a vault proxy, services persist only tokens, and detokenisation happens at a policy-gated API during fulfilment.
Tiered cold events out of Snowflake into S3 Glacier Deep Archive once query patterns showed no reads past 24 months.
A nightly Dagster job exports partitions older than two years as Parquet to S3 Glacier and drops them from the warehouse with an audit row.
Replaced the bespoke SaaS ingestion scripts with Fivetran so that API schema drift stopped paging the data team.
Fivetran connectors land raw tables in Snowflake, dbt sources reference them read-only, and a single orchestration DAG monitors sync cursors.
Adopted Apache Pulsar over Kafka for the cross-region bus once geo-replication and multi-tenant isolation became first-class requirements.
Pulsar brokers run per region with geo-replicated namespaces, functions handle lightweight enrichment, and BookKeeper provides the durable log layer.
Rewrote the pandas transformation layer in SQL running under dbt so that analysts could own the models without touching Python.
dbt models are organised into staging, intermediate, and marts layers, with exposures declared per dashboard and tests on every primary key.
Split the shared Snowflake warehouse into per-team virtual warehouses after noisy-neighbour pipelines starved the finance dashboards.
Each team owns a dedicated virtual warehouse sized by workload, a resource monitor caps credits monthly, and queries route via role-based grants.
Replaced Hive-on-MR with Trino for interactive queries over the lake once analysts started abandoning queries at the 5-minute mark.
Trino coordinators run on Kubernetes, workers autoscale on CPU pressure, and the Iceberg connector points at a shared Glue metastore.
Dropped CSV as the landing format in favour of Parquet after repeated quoting bugs corrupted downstream joins.
Producers write Snappy-compressed Parquet to S3 with hourly prefixes, a Glue crawler registers the tables, and Athena exposes them for ad-hoc queries.
Swapped the legacy cron scheduler for Prefect so that retries and notifications stopped being copy-pasted into every script.
Prefect flows run in an agent pool on ECS, use a Postgres backend for state, and register with a shared work queue per environment.
Adopted Hex for analyst-authored pipelines so that notebooks graduated into versioned, scheduled artifacts without a full rewrite.
Hex projects connect to Snowflake via OAuth, publish scheduled runs, and expose parameterised apps that hand off heavy queries to dbt exposures.
Moved to customer-managed KMS keys for all warehouse object storage after a compliance review flagged tenant-level blast radius concerns.
Each tenant's S3 prefix is encrypted with a dedicated KMS key, Snowflake external tables reference the key id, and revocation happens through a platform API.
Switched event payloads from ad-hoc JSON to Protobuf once producer-consumer drift became the most common data incident.
Protobuf descriptors live in a versioned monorepo, a CI job publishes them to the schema registry, and Flink consumers resolve schemas by fingerprint.
Adopted Trino federation instead of nightly ETL copies between warehouses once product analytics needed joins across Postgres and the lake.
Trino exposes a single SQL surface that federates Postgres, MySQL, Iceberg, and Elasticsearch connectors behind a shared catalog namespace.
Replaced the home-grown webhook buffer service with API Gateway plus Kinesis Firehose once traffic spikes overwhelmed its Redis queue.
API Gateway authenticates webhooks, Firehose buffers events for up to 60 seconds, and a Lambda transforms them into Parquet before landing on S3.
Moved streaming SQL workloads off ksqlDB onto Flink SQL after state store corruption recurred on the 0.29 release.
Flink SQL jobs run on a session cluster, checkpoint to S3 every 30 seconds, and register sinks through the Hive catalog for cross-tool discovery.
Retired Teradata for Databricks SQL once hardware refresh costs crossed the three-year Databricks commit.
Databricks workspaces host Unity Catalog, Delta Lake tables sit on ADLS Gen2, and SQL warehouses serve BI tools behind a Unity-governed metastore.
Chose Flyte over Argo Workflows for ML pipelines because typed interfaces and cached artifacts mattered more than generic container DAGs.
Flyte executions run on a Kubernetes cluster, artifacts persist in an S3-backed data catalog, and task caching keys off input hashes and container digests.
Switched the reverse ETL vendor from Census to Hightouch after their audience-builder better matched the marketing team's workflow.
Hightouch models resolve against Snowflake marts, audiences sync incrementally into Braze and Iterable, and observability flows into the existing Datadog account.
Replaced Maxwell with Debezium for MySQL CDC once we needed transactional metadata and ordered schema change events.
Debezium tails MySQL binlogs, emits events to Kafka topics keyed by primary key, and a downstream Kafka Streams job materialises a compacted changelog.
Swapped Confluent Schema Registry for Apicurio after the self-hosted license model no longer matched the platform budget.
Apicurio runs behind an internal gateway, stores artifacts in Postgres, and integrates with the Kafka connect cluster via the standard Avro serde.
Added Soda Core for SQL-based data checks once shallow freshness alerts kept missing row-level quality regressions.
Soda scans run as post-task steps in Airflow, write check results to a Postgres metadata store, and raise PagerDuty incidents on critical failures.
Moved away from Deequ to Great Expectations once analysts without Scala experience needed to author and review checks.
Great Expectations runs on a dedicated Kubernetes deployment, stores validation results in S3, and renders data docs behind an SSO-protected static site.
Chose OpenMetadata over Datahub for the lineage catalog because the bundled profiler and governance workflow covered a wider surface.
OpenMetadata ingests Airflow, dbt, Snowflake, and Kafka metadata on a schedule, and exposes a GraphQL API that the platform UI embeds for search.
Adopted a central retention service for the lake after legal teams rejected per-dataset manual purging policies.
The retention service reads dataset policies from a YAML registry, issues Iceberg delete queries per partition age, and writes audit rows into a compliance bucket.
Replaced Snowflake time-travel as the long-term archival story with scheduled Parquet exports to keep compliance snapshots vendor-neutral.
A weekly Dagster job exports Snowflake tables as Parquet into a versioned S3 bucket, registers them as Iceberg metadata, and tags the run with a GDPR scope.
Replaced the home-grown HTTP event collector with Segment once mobile SDK work threatened to overflow the product engineering roadmap.
Segment sources land client events into Snowflake via a managed warehouse destination, with PII filters applied via protocols before warehouse delivery.
Picked Apache Beam over Spark Streaming for the cross-runner pipelines so the same code could run on Dataflow and Flink.
Beam pipelines run on Google Dataflow in production and Flink locally, with side inputs backed by a BigQuery reference table refreshed hourly.
Rewrote the heavy transformation scripts from Pandas to Polars after memory spikes crashed the ECS tasks on month-end runs.
Polars jobs stream Parquet batches from S3, group aggregations in a lazy plan, and write results back as partitioned Parquet for downstream dbt models.
Moved reporting workloads off a MySQL read replica onto ClickHouse once dashboard queries started timing out at p95.
ClickHouse runs a sharded cluster behind a chproxy layer, ingests events via Kafka engine tables, and serves BI tools through materialised view projections.
Retired the remaining Luigi DAGs for Airflow 2 once dependency resolution and dynamic task mapping became platform-wide requirements.
Airflow 2 runs on CeleryExecutor with Redis, DAGs live in a git-sync sidecar, and the scheduler uses a highly available Postgres metadata database.
Swapped the Zapier glue for Workato after ops workflows started needing multi-step error handling and audit logs.
Workato recipes pull curated marts from Snowflake, fan out to Salesforce, NetSuite, and Slack, and log every step into a central recipe audit table.
Replaced the Airbyte Postgres source with Debezium once batch-based CDC could no longer meet the 30-second freshness SLA.
Debezium runs on a Kafka Connect cluster, publishes row-level changes to Kafka, and a Spark Structured Streaming job applies them to Delta tables.
Adopted Buf Schema Registry for Protobuf sharing after manual vendored copies drifted across five repos in one quarter.
Buf hosts the canonical Protobuf modules, CI checks enforce breaking-change policies, and code generation fans out into Go, Python, and TypeScript clients.
Moved the data platform's pipeline logs from Datadog to a dedicated Grafana Loki stack because indexed log cost outgrew the per-month budget.
Promtail ships pipeline logs to Loki, Grafana dashboards correlate with Prometheus pipeline metrics, and alerts route through a Grafana OnCall schedule.
Committed to dbt tests as the minimum bar for every new mart after a silent dimension break caused a reporting-day incident.
Every dbt model carries not-null and unique tests on its primary key, plus referential tests on foreign keys, gated by a CI check on pull requests.
Replaced Apache Atlas with Marquez for lineage once the Hadoop-centric data model stopped matching our warehouse-first pipelines.
Marquez stores OpenLineage events in Postgres, exposes a REST API for consumers, and a custom UI overlay surfaces column-level lineage for dbt models.
Built a dedicated subject-request service so that GDPR deletions stopped going through ad-hoc SQL scripts touching every warehouse table.
The subject-request service reads a data map from a catalog, issues tombstone rows into Iceberg tables, and records per-request proofs in a tamper-evident log.
Chose a lakehouse-only archival strategy over cross-region warehouse replicas to avoid doubling the Snowflake storage spend.
Cold partitions live as Iceberg tables on S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, a Unity Catalog external location governs access, and Databricks SQL reads them on demand.
Moved from long-lived API keys to short-lived JWTs after the 2026-01 key leak forced a fleet-wide rotation.
Every service accepts only RS256-signed JWTs with a 10-minute TTL; signing keys rotate nightly from the step-ca issuer.
Retired the hand-rolled KMS wrapper in favour of Vault Transit; custody and audit requirements outgrew the in-house code.
Vault Transit holds every application data key behind AppRole auth; services call encrypt/decrypt endpoints and never see raw key material.
Switched from manual Let's Encrypt renewals to cert-manager after a missed renewal caused a 40-minute outage in February.
cert-manager reconciles Certificate CRs in every namespace, renews 30 days before expiry, and mounts the result as a TLS secret on each pod.
Dropped plaintext secrets in CI environment variables and adopted Vault dynamic database credentials after a log leak exposed a static password.
CI jobs pull ephemeral database roles from Vault at runtime with a 15-minute TTL; static credentials are banned by a repo-level policy check.
Abandoned the flat production VPC and rolled out Cilium network policies after a compromised pod reached the billing subnet laterally.
Cilium enforces default-deny egress in every namespace; allowed flows are declared per service via CiliumNetworkPolicy and tested in CI.
Replaced the AWS managed WAF ruleset with Coraza running the OWASP Core Rule Set; we needed tunable anomaly thresholds the managed one did not expose.
Coraza sits in front of the ingress gateway with CRS 4.0 in blocking mode above an anomaly score of 10; matched requests are tagged and streamed to Loki.
Migrated the perimeter IDS from Snort to Suricata after the Snort rule feed stopped covering our TLS 1.3 traffic patterns.
Suricata runs inline on the north-south edge, consumes the ET Pro ruleset, and drops traffic that matches the `dropable` tag; events go to Elastic.
Split security audit events out of the generic log pipeline after auditors flagged that we could mutate them post-hoc.
Security audit events ship to an append-only Loki tenant with object-lock retention of 7 years; the write role cannot delete or overwrite.
Dropped the nested role hierarchy we had in the admin app and moved to OPA-based attribute checks; the role tree had become impossible to reason about.
The admin backend calls an OPA sidecar on every request; policies are rego files in git, tested with opa test, and evaluated against user attributes plus resource tags.
Retired the corporate VPN for internal tooling after a stolen laptop exposed the shared CIDR; went with an identity-aware proxy instead.
All internal web tools sit behind Pomerium; device posture and SSO identity are evaluated per request and the underlying services only accept traffic from the proxy's mTLS cert.
Replaced the manual device allowlist with TPM-based attestation; operators were sharing device certificates and we could not tell which laptop signed what.
Every workstation enrolls its TPM EK into smallstep; access tokens are only minted after a fresh attestation quote signs a recent nonce from the issuer.
Started signing every internal binary with cosign after a build-server compromise shipped a backdoored CLI to staging.
Release pipelines sign artifacts with keyless cosign using the OIDC token of the GitHub Actions job; verification runs as an admission controller on every cluster.
Version pinning was not enough after the event-stream incident, so we adopted SLSA level 3 provenance for every first-party and vendored dependency.
Build provenance is emitted by the Tekton chain, stored in Rekor, and verified at deploy time; images without a matching in-toto attestation are rejected by the admission webhook.
Nightly-only Trivy scans let a critical CVE sit in production for 14 hours, so we added inline scanning on every push.
Trivy runs in the PR pipeline against the built image and again as a nightly sweep against every running workload; criticals block the merge and page the on-call.
Adopted PagerDuty incident workflows after the December outage ran for two hours with nobody declaring commander.
Every severity-1 page opens a PagerDuty incident channel, assigns a commander from the on-call rotation, and links the standard security-incident runbook automatically.
Host-level LUKS was not enough to satisfy the new PII contract, so we moved to application-layer envelope encryption for customer records.
Each customer record is encrypted with a per-tenant data key; data keys are wrapped by a Vault Transit master key and stored alongside the ciphertext in Postgres.
Moved from opportunistic TLS to mandatory mTLS on every east-west hop after packet captures showed a test service still speaking plaintext in prod.
Istio sidecars enforce strict mTLS on every pod-to-pod connection; the mesh refuses plaintext and certificates come from a short-lived SPIFFE issuer.
Long-lived server sessions were causing replay problems after stolen cookies, so we moved to short access tokens with rotating refresh.
Web clients hold a 10-minute access token and a 24-hour refresh token; the refresh endpoint rotates both on every call and revokes the family on reuse detection.
Killed the local admin account table in favour of Okta SSO after we found three shared logins still in use six months after onboarding Okta.
All internal tools authenticate against Okta via OIDC; group claims drive role mapping and the local account path is disabled at the application level.
Upgraded the password hash from bcrypt at cost 10 to argon2id after the 2026-Q1 GPU cracking benchmark showed bcrypt falling behind.
Argon2id runs with m=64MB, t=3, p=4 inside the auth service; hashes are versioned and re-computed on successful login for users still on the old bcrypt scheme.
The in-house rate limiter collapsed under a 300 Gbps SYN flood in November, so we moved edge DDoS defence to Cloudflare Magic Transit.
Cloudflare Magic Transit announces our /24 and scrubs traffic before forwarding over GRE to the origin routers; the in-house limiter now only handles layer 7 quotas.
Distroless images alone were not enough after a container escape attempt via /tmp, so we tightened the runtime profile as well.
Production pods run as non-root with a read-only root filesystem, drop every Linux capability, and use the `runtime/default` seccomp profile enforced by Kyverno.
Plain UDP DNS inside the VPC exposed us to cache poisoning scenarios, so we switched to DoT with DNSSEC validation on the resolver tier.
Unbound resolvers in every region do DNSSEC validation and forward upstream over DoT to 1.1.1.1; workloads hit the resolvers over an internal Anycast VIP.
The shared-bearer pattern at the API gateway let one partner's leaked token hit other tenants, so we moved to OAuth 2.1 with audience binding.

Kong at the edge validates the JWT signature, checks the `aud` claim against the matched route, and injects a per-tenant identity header that downstream services trust only from the gateway's mTLS peer.
Dropped static service account tokens after one leaked in a core dump; SPIFFE gave us short-lived, workload-bound identities instead.
SPIRE agents attest each workload via the Kubernetes PSAT selector and issue SVIDs with a 1-hour TTL; gRPC servers authenticate peers by SPIFFE ID, not token.
The shared `app` Postgres role made postmortems impossible, so we moved to Vault-issued per-request database roles.
Every request path opens a Postgres connection with a Vault-issued role scoped to the tenant and lifecycle; role grants are generated from the OPA policy bundle at deploy time.
SPF alone kept letting lookalike domains through, so we added DKIM signing and pushed DMARC to p=reject after a full quarter on quarantine.
Outbound mail is signed with a rotating 2048-bit DKIM key per brand domain; DMARC is published at p=reject with aggregate reports piped into a weekly review dashboard.
Cleartext restic repositories on S3 scared the new CISO, so we wrapped every backup with age and kept the key offline.
Backups are written to an S3 bucket with object-lock; restic chunks are encrypted with age using a recipient key whose private half lives only on two offline YubiKeys in the safe.
The iOS team stopped shipping debuggable builds and added Play Integrity / App Attest checks after a reverse-engineered APK hit a test forum.
Release builds pin the API certificate, require a valid App Attest or Play Integrity token on every sensitive call, and refuse to run under a debugger in production flavour.
The 2025 crypto-miner incident got in through an allow-by-default egress rule, so we flipped production to default-deny with an explicit allow-list.
Calico GlobalNetworkPolicies deny all egress in production by default; required destinations are declared per workload and reviewed quarterly against traffic logs.
Admin TOTP was phished twice in six months, so we went passwordless with WebAuthn for anyone with production access.
Admin logins require a WebAuthn assertion from a resident key on a FIDO2 authenticator; password and TOTP paths are disabled for users in the `admins` group at the IdP.
Pulling base images directly from Docker Hub bit us during a rate-limit outage and again with a typosquatted tag, so we routed everything through an internal Harbor proxy.
Harbor proxies Docker Hub and GHCR with on-pull Trivy scanning and cosign signature verification; the cluster's containerd only trusts `registry.corp/*` and refuses other registries.
The legacy `unsafe-inline` CSP let a reflected XSS reach session cookies, so we moved the web app to a strict nonce-based policy.
Every HTML response sets a CSP with `script-src 'self' 'nonce-<per-request>'` and `strict-dynamic`; violations stream to a report-uri endpoint that alerts on novel hashes.
Long-lived SSH keys kept showing up on ex-employee laptops, so we cut over to short-lived SSH certificates signed by Teleport.
Teleport's CA signs SSH certificates valid for 8 hours after SSO + MFA; servers trust only the Teleport CA and the `authorized_keys` path is disabled in sshd_config.
Post-hoc grep sweeps kept missing leaked PII, so we moved redaction up to the logger itself before anything hits disk.
The shared logging wrapper runs a redaction pass on every record using typed field tags; fields marked `sensitive` are hashed with a rotating salt before the log line is serialised.
Running the admin plane next to workloads meant one compromised node could reach the CI controller, so we split it onto a dedicated management cluster.
Admin tools (ArgoCD, Vault, Teleport) run on a separate hardened cluster reachable only via the identity-aware proxy; workload clusters pull from the admin cluster and never push.
Permanent vendor VPN accounts kept outliving their support engagements, so we moved third-party access to a just-in-time broker.
Vendors request time-boxed access through the access broker; on approval, Teleport issues a 4-hour certificate scoped to the specific host and role, and the session is recorded.
Manual PR review for new dependencies missed a GPL library and a known-vulnerable transitive, so we gated it on automated checks.

Every PR that changes a lockfile runs a dependency-review job that fails on GPL/AGPL imports and on advisories above High severity; overrides require a `security-approved` label from the platform team.
Pre-commit secret scanning missed commits from contractors without the hook installed, so we added server-side scanning and a weekly history sweep.
gitleaks runs as a pre-receive hook on the Gitea server and as a nightly full-history sweep; detected secrets auto-open a revocation ticket and block the push.
Rotated out the last long-lived AWS IAM user keys after one leaked via a screenshare; switched CI to OIDC federation instead.
GitHub Actions assumes an AWS role via OIDC with a trust policy bound to the specific repo, branch and environment; the role's session is 1 hour and scoped to a single account.
Wildcard `*:*` policies on legacy services kept surviving reviews, so we enforced permissions boundaries on every role.
Every IAM role in production is attached to a permissions boundary generated from the service's declared needs; Terraform refuses to plan a role without a matching boundary file.
Shared self-hosted runners leaked caches between jobs; a poisoned cache hit the auth service build, so we moved to ephemeral per-job runners.
Each GitHub Actions job spawns a fresh Firecracker microVM via the runner controller; the VM is destroyed at job end and secrets are mounted via short-lived Vault tokens.
An engineer forgot the shared-secret check in a new webhook handler, so we moved verification into a middleware that every handler must pass through.
Inbound webhooks hit a single router that validates the HMAC signature and timestamp window before dispatching to the typed handler; handlers cannot be registered without declaring an allowed signer.
A 30-day manual patch cycle left hosts exposed to a kernel CVE for three weeks, so we moved to continuous automated patching with a canary ring.
Kured drains and reboots nodes within 24 hours of a new kernel package; patches roll through canary, staging and production rings with health gates between each step.
Always-on root access for SRE made SOC 2 reviewers unhappy and caused one real incident, so we introduced a brokered break-glass flow.
Break-glass elevation is requested via the access broker, requires a peer approval in Slack, issues a 60-minute certificate tied to a ticket, and streams the session to an immutable recording bucket.
SameSite=Lax plus a two-week session cookie let a CSRF variant through in staging, so we tightened the cookie policy for the main app.
Session cookies use the `__Host-` prefix with `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict` and a 12-hour expiry; the auth service rejects any request whose cookie fails the prefix invariants.
An annual external pentest missed a staging leak that lived for eight months, so we moved to a quarterly cadence plus continuous attack surface monitoring.
Pentests run quarterly with a rotating vendor; between engagements, an external attack-surface tool scans all known domains daily and files findings directly into the security tracker.
Generic annual training did not move the click rate, so we replaced it with a simulated phishing program tied to just-in-time coaching.
Monthly phishing simulations target all staff; clicks trigger a 10-minute training module immediately and feed a dashboard that drives targeted follow-ups for repeat clickers.
Implicit data classification led to PII ending up in analytics datasets, so we made classification explicit and enforced it through tags.
Every column in the warehouse carries a `classification` tag (public, internal, confidential, restricted); access policies, masking and retention are generated from those tags at deploy time.
Producing SBOMs only for compliance requests meant we could not answer the log4shell question quickly, so we started generating them on every build.
Every build writes a CycloneDX SBOM to the artifact store; a nightly job diffs each SBOM against the previous tag and opens a ticket for any dependency whose advisories changed.
