PostgreSQL's MVCC implementation stores each row version with xmin and xmax transaction identifiers, allowing readers and writers to operate on the same row without blocking each other.
The Linux kernel's completely fair scheduler tracks virtual runtime per task in a red-black tree, selecting the leftmost node on each context switch to approximate ideal multitasking.
Redis stores all keys in a single in-memory hash table per database, with optional persistence via either periodic RDB snapshots or an append-only file log of write commands.
Kubernetes uses etcd as its sole persistent state store, serializing every API object as a key under /registry with optimistic concurrency control through resource versions.
The Raft consensus algorithm elects a single leader per term, and all client writes flow through that leader, which replicates log entries to followers before committing.
HTTP/2 multiplexes concurrent streams over a single TCP connection using binary framing, eliminating the head-of-line blocking problem that plagued HTTP/1.1 pipelining implementations.
TLS 1.3 reduces the full handshake to a single round trip and removes support for legacy cipher suites including RC4, 3DES, and static RSA key exchange.
The CPython global interpreter lock serializes bytecode execution to one thread per process, which limits CPU-bound multithreaded workloads but simplifies the implementation of reference counting.
Docker images are stored as a stack of read-only layers identified by content-addressable digests, with a single thin writable layer created on top when a container starts.
Git stores every tracked file as a zlib-compressed blob addressed by its SHA-1 hash, and commits reference a tree object that recursively names all blobs under the project root.
Elasticsearch builds an inverted index per shard using Lucene segments, and queries that span multiple shards are scatter-gathered by a coordinating node and merged before returning.
The Go garbage collector is a concurrent tri-color mark-sweep collector with short stop-the-world pauses typically under a millisecond even on multi-gigabyte heaps.

PyTorch tensors carry autograd metadata through every operation on the computational graph, and calling backward on a scalar output produces gradients for every leaf tensor with requires_grad enabled.
A transformer self-attention layer computes query, key, and value projections from its input and scales the dot product of queries and keys by the inverse square root of the head dimension.
Kafka partitions a topic into an ordered sequence of immutable log segments per partition, and consumer offsets are committed back to an internal __consumer_offsets topic for replay.

We chose PostgreSQL with pgvector over a dedicated vector database because we already operate Postgres in production and the extra operational surface of another store was not worth the marginal recall gain.
The team decided to standardize on gRPC with protobuf for internal service traffic because schema evolution and strongly typed clients outweighed the debugging friction compared to JSON over HTTP.
We adopted a trunk-based branching model with short-lived feature branches because long-running release branches were accumulating merge debt and delaying security patches by several weeks.

After benchmarking, we selected ScyllaDB instead of Cassandra for the event store because its shard-per-core architecture delivered roughly three times the throughput on our workload with identical hardware.
We are migrating from AWS Lambda to Fargate for the ingestion pipeline because cold starts on large Python containers were adding tail latency that our downstream SLA could not absorb.

The architecture review settled on server-sent events rather than WebSockets for the notification channel because our traffic is unidirectional and SSE flows cleanly through existing HTTP load balancers.

We decided to implement feature flags through LaunchDarkly instead of building in-house because the cost of self-hosted targeting rules, audit logs, and SDK maintenance exceeded two engineer-years of effort.

For the new billing service we chose Temporal over Airflow because the workflows require long-running stateful retries with human-in-the-loop approval, which fit Temporal's programming model more naturally.
The platform team ruled out service mesh sidecars in favor of a gateway-per-namespace pattern because the per-pod memory overhead of Envoy sidecars was unacceptable at our pod density.

We will keep using SQLAlchemy ORM rather than migrate to raw SQL because the test suite relies heavily on session-level transaction rollback for isolation, and rewriting that machinery would stall the roadmap.

After two spikes, we chose to fine-tune a small encoder model locally rather than call a hosted API because throughput requirements combined with per-token cost projected to over twenty thousand dollars monthly.
The data team decided to land raw events in S3 Parquet and run ELT in dbt on Snowflake rather than maintain a Spark cluster, trading some flexibility for an order-of-magnitude lower ops burden.
We picked Ruff over Flake8 plus Black as our combined linter and formatter because Ruff runs roughly a hundred times faster on our monorepo and covers the superset of rules we already enforce.

The security working group decided to enforce mTLS between internal services through SPIFFE identities instead of shared static certificates, because rotation of static certs had already caused two production incidents.

We chose to use FastAPI for the new public API rather than extend the existing Flask service because dependency injection and automatic OpenAPI generation meaningfully reduce the boilerplate our team rewrites per endpoint.
I prefer writing database migrations with Alembic autogenerate as a starting point, then manually editing the output to add data backfills and verify that no unintended index changes snuck in.

My default is to use pytest fixtures with explicit scope rather than setUp and tearDown methods, because fixture composition keeps integration tests readable even when they touch several subsystems at once.

I like running ripgrep over find plus grep for large repositories because the default respect for gitignore and the multi-threaded search deliver results an order of magnitude faster on any codebase I use.
When writing shell scripts I always set errexit, nounset, and pipefail at the top because silent failures in production cron jobs have bitten me too many times to count.
For container debugging I prefer running an ephemeral distroless image with a shell sidecar rather than baking busybox into production images, because it keeps the attack surface minimal.

I write commit messages in the imperative mood following the Conventional Commits specification because it makes the changelog generation deterministic and pairs well with automated semantic versioning.
My preferred editor configuration is Neovim with a minimal Lua config using lazy.nvim for plugin management, because I dislike opaque startup times and want every loaded plugin to justify its cost.
I prefer explicit type hints on all public function signatures in Python, even when mypy could infer them, because hints serve as primary documentation and catch refactoring mistakes early in CI.

For dependency management in Python I use uv with a locked pyproject.toml because it resolves and installs orders of magnitude faster than pip plus pip-tools and produces deterministic cross-platform lockfiles.

I prefer structured logging with JSON lines over human-readable log formats in all production services because downstream aggregation in Loki or Elasticsearch is strictly cheaper when the format is machine parseable.

When writing tests I prefer table-driven style with clearly named cases rather than one assertion per test function, because it captures coverage intent compactly without sacrificing readable failure messages.
I like pinning container base images to a specific digest rather than a floating tag because tag mutation has caused me reproducibility problems that took hours to diagnose across environments.
I prefer using just or make for task running over shell scripts scattered across a repository because a single discoverable entry point lowers onboarding friction for new contributors.

For API documentation I favor generating the OpenAPI spec from code annotations rather than hand-writing YAML, because drift between the implementation and the contract is the most common source of integration bugs.
I prefer reviewing pull requests on the command line with gh pr diff and a local checkout rather than in the browser UI, because I can run tests and explore adjacent code without context switching.
The checkout service is dropping requests under load because the connection pool to the payment processor is configured with a hard cap of twenty, and burst traffic regularly exceeds that limit.
Our nightly ETL job has started timing out after a schema migration, and the new bigint primary key caused the join planner to fall back to a hash join that spills to disk.
The Kubernetes cluster is OOM-killing the ingestion pods every few hours because memory limits were copied from the old VM sizing and never adjusted for the heavier workload after the feature launch.
We are seeing intermittent 502 responses from the API gateway that correlate with upstream keepalive timeouts, suggesting the gateway is reusing connections that the backend has already closed.
The fine-tuning run keeps diverging around the second epoch because the learning rate warmup is too short, and gradient norms briefly spike above the clip threshold before stabilizing.
Our Postgres replica lag has been growing unboundedly during business hours because a long-running analytical query on the primary is holding locks that block WAL application on the follower.
The CI pipeline on the main branch is flaky because the integration tests depend on system clock ordering, and GitHub-hosted runners occasionally step time backwards during VM migration.

The search index is returning stale results for roughly ten minutes after a product update because the change-data-capture pipeline has a batch flush interval that compounds with Elasticsearch refresh latency.
Training throughput on the GPU cluster has collapsed to half its expected value because NCCL is falling back to TCP transport instead of using the RDMA fabric that the nodes were provisioned with.
The mobile app is crashing at startup for a subset of Android users because a native dependency silently requires armv8 instructions that older devices on the long tail do not support.
We are leaking file descriptors in the log shipper because the rotation handler is not closing the previous file when the underlying inode changes, leading to an eventual crash after several days.

The rate limiter is blocking legitimate traffic because its sliding window is keyed by a forwarded IP that is often set to the reverse proxy's own address when the trusted-proxy list is misconfigured.
Our vector search recall has quietly dropped on a specific tenant because their embeddings were re-indexed with a different model version, and the ANN index still points at the older centroids.
The deployment pipeline is silently deploying stale container images because the image tag in the Helm values file is not updated atomically with the digest pinned in the admission controller policy.

We are seeing a steady increase in 5xx responses from the authentication service that correlates with JWT verification time, which points at an expanded JWKS cache miss rate after a recent key rotation.

The platform is organized as a set of independently deployable services communicating over gRPC, fronted by an Envoy edge proxy that terminates TLS and performs authentication through a sidecar policy agent.
Our data plane follows a medallion lakehouse pattern, landing raw CDC events in a bronze layer, curating them into silver tables with dbt, and materializing gold aggregates consumed by BI tools.

The ingestion pipeline uses a claim-check pattern: producers write large payloads to object storage, publish only the reference on Kafka, and consumers dereference the claim when they are ready to process it.
The authentication subsystem is split into an identity provider, a token service issuing signed JWTs, and a policy decision point evaluating Rego rules against request context at ingress.

Our billing system applies event sourcing: every state change is an immutable event written to a durable log, and current balances are projected into read models rebuilt whenever the projection logic evolves.
The frontend is a single-page application shipped as static assets behind a CDN, hydrating against a GraphQL gateway that fans out to several internal REST services and caches responses in Redis.

The machine learning serving stack runs Triton as the model server behind a KServe control plane, with model artifacts stored in MinIO and a Kafka feedback loop feeding online metrics back to training.

Our search architecture places a primary Elasticsearch cluster for user-facing queries, a secondary cluster for analytics, and a replication bridge that keeps them in sync through a cross-cluster replication link.

The observability stack consists of OpenTelemetry collectors on every node, forwarding metrics to Prometheus, traces to Tempo, and logs to Loki, with Grafana as the single-pane-of-glass visualization layer.

The notification system uses a publish-subscribe core on NATS JetStream with separate consumer groups per channel, allowing email, push, and SMS workers to scale independently based on their downstream latency budgets.

Our multi-tenant SaaS uses a shared database with a tenant_id column on every table, enforced through Postgres row-level security policies and a connection-level SET that establishes the current tenant per request.
The storage tier is structured as a log-structured merge tree with memtables in RAM, immutable sorted string tables on disk, and a background compactor that merges levels to bound read amplification.

The CI/CD architecture uses GitHub Actions for build and test, Argo CD for pull-based deployment, and a promotion pipeline that moves signed container digests through staging, canary, and production clusters.

Our retrieval-augmented generation pipeline chunks documents with a semantic splitter, indexes them into a hybrid store combining BM25 and dense embeddings, and reranks top candidates with a cross-encoder before generation.

The payment service follows a hexagonal architecture: the domain core is framework-free, adapters on the edge translate to Stripe and internal ledger APIs, and tests exercise the core through in-memory adapter fakes.

We completed the migration of the primary database from MySQL 5.7 to PostgreSQL 16 last Thursday, cutting over during a two-hour maintenance window with less than thirty seconds of write unavailability.
The platform team shipped the first production rollout of the new service mesh this sprint, bringing fifteen services under mutual TLS with zero customer-visible downtime during the switchover.

We closed out the quarter by reducing median API tail latency from three hundred milliseconds to ninety milliseconds after the query plan caching and connection-pool tuning work landed in production last week.

The fine-tuning team delivered the first internal release of the in-house embedding model, hitting 93 percent recall at ten on our retrieval benchmark, a four-point improvement over the hosted baseline.

We finished migrating every workload off the legacy monolith last Friday, decommissioned the final EC2 auto-scaling group, and retired roughly forty thousand lines of code that had not changed in two years.

The observability rollout reached full coverage this week, with every service emitting OpenTelemetry traces and the engineering organization now capable of tracing any request end to end through a single Grafana URL.

We hit general availability for the multi-region active-active deployment yesterday, with synthetic probes confirming sub-fifty-millisecond failover across us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-2 during the scheduled game-day exercise.

The mobile team shipped version 5.0 to production this morning, completing the twelve-month rewrite onto Kotlin Multiplatform and eliminating the last Objective-C code from the iOS target along the way.
We closed the last blocker for SOC 2 Type II this afternoon, completing the audit evidence collection for the final control family and putting the formal report on track for issuance next month.

The data platform reached feature parity with the old warehouse last week, and every downstream dashboard has been validated byte-for-byte, allowing us to schedule the decommission for the end of the quarter.

We completed the zero-downtime rollout of the new authentication stack this sprint, migrating all forty million active sessions to the new token format over a seven-day gradual cutover with no support escalations.
The deep learning team finished the pretraining run for the 7B parameter model yesterday, logging a final validation loss of 1.82 after processing two trillion tokens across the production GPU fleet.

We shipped the new code review automation to the entire engineering org last Monday, and it is already catching roughly thirty percent of the nit-level comments that previously consumed human reviewer time.

The infrastructure team completed the rollout of IPv6 dual-stack across every production subnet this quarter, closing the last remaining item on the multi-year networking modernization roadmap owned by the platform group.

We landed the last piece of the encryption-at-rest migration yesterday, rotating all customer-managed keys through the new KMS hierarchy and closing out the compliance finding that had been open for roughly eighteen months.
According to RFC 9110 section 9.3.1, the HTTP GET method is defined as safe and idempotent, meaning a correctly implemented GET request does not cause observable state change on the origin server.

Per RFC 7519, a JSON Web Token consists of three base64url-encoded segments — header, payload, and signature — joined by dot separators, as specified in the JWT proposed standard published by the IETF.

The PostgreSQL 16 documentation chapter on Write-Ahead Logging states that WAL records must be flushed to durable storage before the corresponding dirty data pages, which is the mechanism enabling crash recovery.

Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, published at NeurIPS 2017 as arXiv:1706.03762, introduced the Transformer architecture based on scaled dot-product self-attention without recurrence or convolution.
The Kubernetes API reference for version 1.29 specifies that a Pod's restartPolicy field applies to every container in the Pod and defaults to Always when the field is omitted from the manifest.

According to the CUDA C++ Programming Guide published by NVIDIA, threads within the same warp execute instructions in lockstep, and divergent control flow across those threads is serialized by the hardware scheduler.
As established in RFC 8446, TLS version 1.3 completes a full handshake in a single round trip and removes support for legacy cipher suites including RC4, 3DES, and static RSA key transport.

The Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 specification maintained at semver.org defines that the MAJOR version must be incremented for incompatible API changes while MINOR is reserved for backward-compatible additions of functionality.

According to Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann, linearizability is the strongest real-time consistency guarantee and is fundamentally more expensive to provide than sequential or causal consistency in distributed systems.

The Raft consensus paper by Ongaro and Ousterhout, published at USENIX ATC 2014 under the title In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, defines leader election, log replication, and safety in clear terms.
My apartment lease runs from the first of September through the end of August, and the landlord charges a flat fee for any late rent payment submitted past the fifth.
The family cabin in Vermont was built by my grandfather in 1962 using lumber milled from spruce trees he cleared off the back lot himself.
My driver's license expires on my birthday in 2029, and the state requires an in-person vision test before it can be renewed for another eight years.
My partner grew up bilingual in Portuguese and English because her mother moved from Lisbon to Boston at the age of twenty-three for graduate school.
The oak tree in the front yard is about ninety years old, according to the previous owner who counted the rings on a fallen limb during a storm cleanup.
My father retired from the postal service in 2018 after thirty-four years of delivering mail along the same rural route in eastern Pennsylvania.
Our dog Biscuit is a nine-year-old rescue beagle who weighs twenty-six pounds and takes a daily thyroid tablet with his breakfast.
The local farmers market operates every Saturday from May through October in the public library parking lot, and nearly forty vendors set up each week.
The Amazon rainforest produces roughly six percent of the planet's atmospheric oxygen and stores an estimated one hundred fifty billion tonnes of carbon in its biomass.
The human genome contains approximately three billion base pairs distributed across twenty-three chromosome pairs, with protein-coding genes making up less than two percent of the total.
Mount Everest grows roughly four millimeters taller each year due to the ongoing collision between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates along the Himalayan range.
Honeybees communicate the direction and distance of nectar sources through a figure-eight waggle dance whose angle encodes the sun's bearing relative to the flowers.
The Library of Congress in Washington holds over one hundred seventy million items across its collections, making it the largest library in the world by volume.
Saturn's rings are composed almost entirely of water ice particles ranging from dust grains to boulders several meters across, orbiting within a band only tens of meters thick.
The Great Barrier Reef stretches roughly two thousand three hundred kilometers along the northeastern coast of Australia and is visible from low earth orbit.
I decided to switch from a gas stove to an induction cooktop when we remodel the kitchen next spring because of the faster heating and easier cleanup.

After weighing tuition versus scholarships, I chose the in-state university over the private college and will redirect the savings toward a down payment on a condo.
My sister and I agreed to split the cost of hiring a caregiver for our mother three afternoons a week rather than placing her in assisted living.
I decided to stop drinking coffee after two in the afternoon because late caffeine was clearly fragmenting my sleep according to the sleep tracker data.
We picked the smaller pediatric clinic across town over the large hospital network because their same-day appointment availability has been much more consistent.
The World Health Organization decided in 2022 to add monkeypox to its list of public health emergencies of international concern, triggering coordinated surveillance across member states.
In 1969 NASA chose lunar orbit rendezvous over direct ascent for Apollo missions because it dramatically reduced the mass that had to be launched from Earth.
The European Central Bank decided to maintain its deposit facility rate unchanged through the first quarter of 2026 while monitoring core inflation in the eurozone.
The International Astronomical Union decided in 2006 to reclassify Pluto as a dwarf planet after establishing a formal definition requiring orbital clearance of surrounding debris.
The Japanese government decided to begin releasing treated water from the Fukushima Daiichi site into the Pacific in 2023 following IAEA safety review.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change chose in its sixth assessment cycle to present scenario pathways rather than a single probabilistic forecast of future warming.
The Nobel Committee in Stockholm decided to award the 2024 prize in physics jointly to two researchers whose foundational work laid the groundwork for artificial neural networks.
I strongly prefer cooking with cast iron over nonstick pans because the seasoning improves with use and I can move the same pan from stovetop to oven without worry.
My morning routine is non-negotiable: I like black tea rather than coffee, a short walk rather than a run, and thirty minutes of reading before checking any messages.
When traveling I would rather stay in small family-run guesthouses than chain hotels because the hosts usually point me toward the best local food spots.
For weekend dinners I prefer slow braises and stews over quick sears because the house smells wonderful for hours and leftovers actually taste better the next day.
I like paperback novels much more than e-readers for fiction, though I happily use the tablet for cookbooks and technical references that benefit from search.
My dad prefers watching baseball on the radio to watching on television because the announcers paint a more vivid picture and the pace feels less frantic.
I would rather hike an unfamiliar trail in early spring than midsummer because the lack of foliage makes it easier to read the landscape and navigate without a map.
When it comes to gifts, I like handwritten letters and homemade food far more than anything bought in a store, even if the store-bought item costs more.
Many classical musicians prefer gut strings over synthetic ones for baroque repertoire because the warmer overtones better match the tonal expectations of period performance.
Field ecologists tend to prefer camera traps over live trapping when studying nocturnal mammals because the method is far less stressful for the animals and yields longer observation windows.
Sommeliers typically prefer decanting older reds for thirty minutes rather than an hour because the delicate aromatics of aged wine can dissipate with too much air exposure.
Astronomers generally prefer ground-based adaptive optics for nearby targets but still favor space telescopes like Hubble and JWST for deep-field infrared surveys.
Pastry chefs often prefer European-style butter with higher fat content over American supermarket butter because lamination for croissants becomes noticeably more forgiving.
Professional translators working with poetry tend to prefer preserving rhythm and image over literal fidelity because readers respond more strongly to cadence than to exact word choice.
Long-distance runners often prefer negative splits over even pacing in marathons because finishing with a faster second half tends to correlate with better overall times and lower injury rates.
The upstairs bathroom has been leaking into the ceiling below for at least a week, and the drywall is now showing a brown ring roughly the size of a dinner plate.
My car has been making a grinding noise whenever I brake at low speed, and the dealership told me the rear rotors are warped and will need to be replaced.
My son has been struggling with math homework all semester because the teacher moved on from long division before he had fully grasped place-value reasoning.
The backyard fence collapsed during last week's windstorm, and the neighbor's dog has already crossed into our yard three times looking for our compost bin.
I have been dealing with chronic wrist pain that flares up every afternoon at my desk, and the physical therapist suspects a repetitive strain injury from poor posture.
The basement floods every spring because the exterior grading slopes toward the foundation on the east side, and last year's sump pump could not keep up.
My mother has been forgetting medication doses more frequently, and her weekly pill organizer is not enough structure anymore to keep her schedule reliable.
Our home internet drops out every evening around seven, and the modem logs suggest the cable segment is being oversubscribed once the neighborhood streams.
Antibiotic resistance is spreading faster than new drug development pipelines can keep up, and several gram-negative pathogens now have no reliably effective treatment options.
Coral reefs worldwide are experiencing mass bleaching events at accelerating intervals because sea surface temperatures are rising beyond the thermal tolerance of symbiotic zooxanthellae.
Urban light pollution has reduced visible star counts in most major cities to fewer than two dozen, disrupting migratory bird navigation and circadian biology in several species.
Groundwater aquifers across the American Southwest are being depleted faster than natural recharge can replenish them, threatening both agricultural output and municipal water supplies.
Microplastic contamination has been detected in human placental tissue, raising unresolved questions about long-term developmental effects that current toxicology studies cannot yet answer.
The global bee population has declined significantly over the past two decades due to combined pressures from neonicotinoid pesticides, Varroa mites, and habitat loss.
Arctic permafrost is thawing at rates that release stored methane faster than climate models anticipated, creating a feedback loop that accelerates further warming.

My monthly budget splits net income fifty, thirty, and twenty percent across fixed bills, flexible spending, and brokerage transfers, with a separate buffer account holding one full month of expenses.
Our household laundry system runs on a three-basket rotation by color in the bedroom, with a single hamper downstairs for towels and linens washed on Sundays.
The family calendar layers a shared Google account for appointments, a paper whiteboard in the kitchen for weekly meals, and a private notebook for each parent's work commitments.
My pantry is organized by meal type on four shelves: breakfast grains up top, baking supplies middle, savory staples below that, and snacks at eye level for the kids.
The garden is divided into four raised beds rotated annually through tomatoes, brassicas, legumes, and cover crops to keep soil-borne disease pressure manageable.
Our emergency plan designates one out-of-state relative as the family contact, a meeting spot at the corner park, and a waterproof binder holding document copies in the hall closet.
My weekly meal prep splits Sunday afternoon into three stages: roast a tray of vegetables, cook two grains, and portion five protein servings into glass containers for the week.
The household finances run on a two-account structure where one checking account receives all paychecks and a second account covers discretionary spending after the monthly auto-transfer.

The three-branch structure of the United States federal government distributes legislative, executive, and judicial authority across Congress, the presidency, and the federal courts with explicit checks on each branch.

A coral reef ecosystem is structured in vertical zones from the reef crest down through the fore-reef slope, with distinct communities of fish and invertebrates adapted to each depth and light regime.
The human circulatory system runs as a double loop: the pulmonary circuit exchanges gases between heart and lungs while the systemic circuit delivers oxygenated blood to the rest of the body.
A Gothic cathedral distributes its load through pointed arches, flying buttresses, and ribbed vaults, which together allowed medieval builders to open walls for large stained glass windows.
The scientific method cycles through observation, hypothesis, prediction, experimentation, and analysis, with each iteration refining the working model against empirical evidence.
A symphony orchestra is organized into four sections — strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion — arranged on stage by volume and blend so the conductor can balance the overall sound.
The Dewey Decimal System partitions all of human knowledge into ten top-level classes, each subdivided into ten divisions and further into ten sections for finer cataloging.
Last weekend I finally finished refinishing the hardwood floors in the living room, capping off a six-month renovation that included the kitchen cabinets and the downstairs bathroom.
My daughter learned to ride her bike without training wheels on the first warm Saturday of April after two weeks of wobbling practice in the cul-de-sac.

My grandmother celebrated her ninetieth birthday in March, with four generations of the family gathered at her home in rural Michigan for a surprise afternoon party.

My son took his first steps on the kitchen tile three days before his first birthday, wobbling from the refrigerator to my chair while laughing the entire way.
Humanity first reached the summit of Mount Everest in 1953 when Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay climbed the final ridge and planted the flags of four nations at the top.
The Human Genome Project released its first complete draft sequence in 2001, marking a fundamental milestone in molecular biology that took over a decade and three billion dollars.

The Large Hadron Collider announced the discovery of the Higgs boson in July 2012, completing the standard model of particle physics after nearly five decades of theoretical prediction.

According to the appraisal report filed by Sanderson Valuation Associates on March 14, 2025, the property's fair market value is recorded as four hundred twenty-seven thousand dollars.
My pediatrician's clinical note dated September 8th, 2025 states that my daughter's growth curve is tracking in the seventieth percentile for height and the sixtieth for weight.
The homeowners association covenant, section 4.2, specifies that exterior paint colors must be selected from the approved palette listed in Appendix B of the governing document.
My employment contract, clause 11 on remote work, allows up to two in-person days per month to be waived with written approval from the direct supervisor.
According to the veterinary records from Brookline Animal Hospital on February 2nd, 2025, our dog's rabies vaccination remains valid through February of 2028.
The CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, volume 73, issue 12, documents the seasonal influenza hospitalization rates for the 2024 through 2025 flu season across reporting states.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Sixth Assessment Report, working group one chapter four, projects a likely range of global mean surface temperature rise through 2100 under several scenarios.
Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species,' first edition published in 1859, introduces the mechanism of natural selection in chapter four under the heading of struggle for existence.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook, 2024 through 2025 edition, projects employment for registered nurses to grow by six percent over the coming decade.
According to the Oxford English Dictionary, third edition entry for 'serendipity', the word was coined by Horace Walpole in a letter written on January 28th, 1754.

Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785), formulates the categorical imperative as acting only on that maxim whereby one can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.
A moral agent ought to act only on maxims that the agent can consistently will to hold as universal laws binding on every rational being.

John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (Harvard University Press, 1971), argues that principles of justice are those that would be chosen by rational parties behind a veil of ignorance in the original position.
Fair principles of social justice are the principles that rational people would agree to if they had to choose without knowing their own social position, talents, or conception of the good.

Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (Oxford University Press, 1984), argues that personal identity over time consists in psychological continuity and connectedness rather than in a further fact about a persisting self.
The persistence of a person over time is constituted by overlapping chains of memory, intention, and psychological connection rather than by any extra metaphysical fact about a continuing self.

G. E. M. Anscombe, 'Modern Moral Philosophy', Philosophy 33 (1958) 1-19, argues that the concepts of moral obligation and moral duty should be jettisoned until an adequate philosophy of psychology is available.
The modern vocabulary of moral obligation and moral duty makes little sense outside a theological framework, and ethics should be rebuilt on a theory of human flourishing and the virtues.
Edmund Gettier, 'Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?', Analysis 23 (1963) 121-123, presents counterexamples showing that justified true belief is insufficient for knowledge.
A person can have a justified true belief without having knowledge, because the belief can be true only by accident relative to its justification.

Thomas Nagel, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?', The Philosophical Review 83 (1974) 435-450, argues that consciousness has an essentially subjective character that escapes any objective physicalist reduction.
Conscious experience has an irreducibly subjective character, and no purely objective description of neural or physical processes can fully capture what it is like to be a conscious subject.

David Chalmers, 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness', Journal of Consciousness Studies 2 (1995) 200-219, distinguishes the easy problems of cognition from the hard problem of explaining phenomenal experience.
Explaining why physical processes in the brain are accompanied by subjective experience at all is a distinct and harder problem than explaining cognitive functions like attention or reportability.

Frank Jackson, 'Epiphenomenal Qualia', Philosophical Quarterly 32 (1982) 127-136, presents the Mary thought experiment to argue that complete physical knowledge leaves out facts about phenomenal experience.

A scientist raised in a black-and-white room who knows every physical fact about color vision still learns something new when she sees red for the first time, suggesting that not all facts are physical facts.
Hilary Putnam, 'The Meaning of Meaning', in Mind, Language and Reality (Cambridge University Press, 1975), uses the Twin Earth thought experiment to argue that meanings are not purely in the head.

Two speakers in internally identical brain states can nonetheless mean different things by the same word when their physical and social environments differ, so linguistic meaning depends in part on the external world.
Saul Kripke, Naming and Necessity (Harvard University Press, 1980), defends a causal-historical theory of reference for proper names against the descriptivist view.

Proper names typically refer to their bearers through a causal-historical chain reaching back to an initial baptism, rather than by expressing some set of descriptions that uniquely identify the bearer.
W. V. O. Quine, 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism', The Philosophical Review 60 (1951) 20-43, attacks the analytic-synthetic distinction and reductionist verificationism.
There is no principled distinction between purely analytic truths and synthetic empirical truths, and our beliefs face the tribunal of experience only as a holistic web rather than one by one.

Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (University of Chicago Press, 1962), argues that mature sciences develop through alternating periods of normal science and revolutionary paradigm shifts.
Scientific progress is not uniformly cumulative but proceeds through long stretches of normal puzzle-solving within a shared framework punctuated by revolutionary changes in fundamental assumptions.
Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery (Hutchinson, 1959), argues that the distinctive mark of scientific theories is falsifiability rather than verifiability.
A theory counts as genuinely scientific only if it makes predictions that could in principle be falsified by observation, since no finite set of confirming instances can establish a universal claim.
David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739-40), Book III, Part I, Section I, observes the shift from 'is' to 'ought' propositions and questions its justification.
A normative conclusion about what ought to be the case cannot be validly derived from purely descriptive premises about what is the case without the aid of some further normative premise.
G. E. Moore, Principia Ethica (Cambridge University Press, 1903), deploys the open-question argument against identifying the good with any natural property.

For any proposed natural property identified with goodness, it remains a genuinely open question whether things with that property are good, suggesting that goodness is not identical with any such property.
John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism (Parker, Son and Bourn, 1863), defends the greatest happiness principle as the foundation of morals.
Actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness and wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness, with happiness understood as pleasure and the absence of pain.

Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), proposes a felicific calculus measuring pleasures and pains by intensity, duration, certainty, and related features.

The moral evaluation of an action depends on the aggregate of pleasures and pains it produces, assessed along dimensions such as intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent.
Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, identifies the human good with eudaimonia, understood as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life.
The human good is a life of activity exercising the characteristic excellences of a rational being, sustained throughout a complete life rather than experienced in isolated moments.

Peter Singer, 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality', Philosophy and Public Affairs 1 (1972) 229-243, argues that affluent people are morally obligated to give substantially to prevent suffering from famine.

If one can prevent serious suffering at no comparable moral cost, one is morally required to do so, which implies that affluent individuals are obligated to donate a large share of their resources to relieve extreme poverty.

Judith Jarvis Thomson, 'A Defense of Abortion', Philosophy and Public Affairs 1 (1971) 47-66, uses the violinist thought experiment to argue that even granting fetal personhood, abortion can be morally permissible.

Even if the fetus is granted the moral status of a person, a pregnant person is not always morally required to sustain that life with her own body, because no one has an unconditional right to use another person's body.
Philippa Foot, 'The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect', Oxford Review 5 (1967) 5-15, introduces the trolley case and distinguishes doing from allowing harm.
There is a morally significant distinction between directly killing a smaller number of people as a means and merely diverting a harm so that a smaller number are killed as a side effect.
Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Basic Books, 1974), defends a minimal state and an entitlement theory of distributive justice based on just acquisition and transfer.

A distribution of holdings is just if it arises from an initially just acquisition of unowned resources followed by voluntary transfers, and redistribution beyond what a minimal state requires violates individual rights.
Ronald Dworkin, Taking Rights Seriously (Harvard University Press, 1977), argues that individual rights function as trumps over collective goals grounded in background utility.

Individual moral rights set side constraints that override ordinary appeals to aggregate welfare, so a government may not violate an individual's right merely because doing so would maximize overall social utility.
John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (John W. Parker and Son, 1859), defends the harm principle as the sole legitimate ground for coercive interference with individual liberty.
The only ground on which society is entitled to restrict an adult's liberty against his will is to prevent harm to others, and neither his own good nor moral disapproval by others suffices.
H. L. A. Hart, 'Positivism and the Separation of Law and Morals', Harvard Law Review 71 (1958) 593-629, defends legal positivism against Lon Fuller's natural law critique.
The existence and content of a legal system is one question and its moral merit is another, so a rule can be legally valid even when it fails to satisfy moral demands.

John Searle, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3 (1980) 417-457, uses the Chinese Room thought experiment to argue that syntactic symbol manipulation is insufficient for semantic understanding.

A system that produces intelligent-seeming responses purely by manipulating symbols according to formal rules does not thereby understand the language it appears to use, because syntax does not suffice for semantics.
Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Mind 59 (1950) 433-460, proposes the imitation game as an operational test for machine intelligence.
A reasonable operational criterion for machine intelligence is whether a machine can hold a text-based conversation indistinguishable from that of a human interlocutor to a blinded judge.
Daniel Dennett, The Intentional Stance (MIT Press, 1987), argues that ascribing beliefs and desires is a predictive strategy rather than the discovery of intrinsic mental states.

Treating a system as a rational agent that holds beliefs and desires is a predictive strategy that works whenever doing so yields reliable predictions of behavior, independently of the system's internal composition.
David Lewis, On the Plurality of Worlds (Blackwell, 1986), defends modal realism on which possible worlds are concrete entities as real as our own world.
A claim that something is possible is to be analyzed as saying that there is some concrete world, spatiotemporally isolated from ours, in which that thing is the case.
Saul Kripke, Naming and Necessity (Harvard University Press, 1980), argues that identity statements involving rigid designators, such as 'water is H2O', are necessary a posteriori truths.
Some truths can be known only through empirical investigation and yet are necessary, because an identity between two rigid designators holds in every possible world in which either refers.
W. V. O. Quine, 'On What There Is', Review of Metaphysics 2 (1948) 21-38, proposes that to be is to be the value of a bound variable in our best regimented theory.
Our ontological commitments are just those entities that must be taken to exist for our best regimented theories of the world to come out true, identified by what their quantifiers range over.
David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV, poses the problem of the rational justification of inductive inference.
No non-circular argument shows that the future will resemble the past, since any such argument either presupposes induction or relies on an ungrounded principle of the uniformity of nature.
Nelson Goodman, Fact, Fiction, and Forecast (Harvard University Press, 1955), introduces the predicate 'grue' to pose the new riddle of induction.

Any body of evidence that confirms 'all emeralds are green' equally confirms a gerrymandered hypothesis such as 'all emeralds are grue', so inductive support depends on which predicates are taken as projectible.
Bernard Williams, 'Internal and External Reasons', in Moral Luck (Cambridge University Press, 1981), argues that all genuine reasons for action must connect to an agent's existing motivational set.
A consideration counts as a reason for an agent to act only if a sound deliberative route leads from that agent's existing desires, commitments, and projects to the action in question.

T. M. Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other (Harvard University Press, 1998), defends a contractualist account on which an act is wrong if its performance would be disallowed by any principle no one could reasonably reject.
An act is morally wrong just when it is forbidden by some principle for the general regulation of behavior that no one, suitably motivated to find terms of cooperation, could reasonably reject.
Thomas Nagel, The View from Nowhere (Oxford University Press, 1986), explores the tension between subjective and objective standpoints in epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics.
Human thought occupies both an engaged, subjective standpoint and a detached, impersonal standpoint, and many philosophical problems arise from the difficulty of integrating the two views.
Plato, Republic, Books II-IV, argues that justice in the soul consists in each part performing its proper function under the rule of reason.
Justice in the individual consists in a harmonious ordering of rational, spirited, and appetitive parts of the soul, with reason ruling the other two parts.
Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 94, articulates natural law as the rational creature's participation in the eternal law.
Basic moral principles are grasped by practical reason reflecting on the natural inclinations of rational beings toward goods such as life, sociability, and knowledge.
Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (Andrew Crooke, 1651), Part I Chapter 13, describes life in the state of nature as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'.
In the absence of a common power able to enforce peace, human beings would live in a condition of war of all against all in which life would be insecure, impoverished, and brief.
John Locke, Two Treatises of Government (Awnsham Churchill, 1689), Second Treatise Chapter V, grounds private property in the mixing of one's labor with an unowned thing.
A person acquires a rightful property in a previously unowned natural resource when he mixes his own labor with it, provided that enough and as good is left for others.
Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Du Contrat Social (Marc-Michel Rey, 1762), argues that legitimate political authority rests on the general will of the people.
Legitimate political authority is grounded in a general will that aims at the common good of the political community, as distinct from the aggregated private wills of its members.
G. W. F. Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807), Section IV.A, presents the master-slave dialectic as a stage in the development of self-consciousness through mutual recognition.

Self-consciousness develops through a struggle for recognition in which the relation between a dominating and a dominated consciousness ultimately proves unstable because genuine self-understanding requires recognition by an equal.
Friedrich Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality (C. G. Naumann, 1887), traces the historical origins of moral concepts such as good, evil, guilt, and bad conscience.
Modern moral concepts have a contingent historical origin in particular social practices and psychological dynamics, and tracing that origin can expose their tacit assumptions and power relations.
Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (Blackwell, 1953), sections 243-315, presents the private language argument against the possibility of a purely private sensation language.

A language whose words refer only to sensations knowable to a single speaker cannot support a genuine distinction between correctly and incorrectly applying a term, and so cannot be a language at all.
Gottlob Frege, 'Uber Sinn und Bedeutung', Zeitschrift fur Philosophie und philosophische Kritik 100 (1892) 25-50, distinguishes sense (Sinn) from reference (Bedeutung) for linguistic expressions.
Two expressions can share a referent while differing in the cognitive mode of presentation associated with them, so the meaning of an expression includes more than just the object it picks out.
Carl Hempel and Paul Oppenheim, 'Studies in the Logic of Explanation', Philosophy of Science 15 (1948) 135-175, articulate the deductive-nomological model of scientific explanation.

On one influential view, a scientific explanation of an event is a sound deductive argument whose premises include at least one general law and whose conclusion is a statement of the event to be explained.
David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section X, argues that testimony can never establish a miracle as more probable than its violation of the laws of nature.

Since a miracle by definition is a violation of a well-established law of nature, the evidence against such a violation is always stronger than any human testimony in its favor, so belief in miracles on testimony alone is unwarranted.

John Dewey, Art as Experience (Minton, Balch, 1934), argues that aesthetic value consists in the consummatory quality of an experience rather than in intrinsic features of a privileged class of objects.
What makes an experience aesthetic is its having a unified, consummatory quality in which means and ends are integrated, rather than the presence of some special class of fine-art objects.
Immanuel Kant, Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790), Book II, analyzes the feeling of the sublime as a response to objects that exceed our capacity for sensible representation.
The feeling of the sublime arises when the imagination is overwhelmed by something vast or powerful, and reason then recognizes its own supersensible vocation in the very failure of sensory grasp.
Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (J. Johnson, 1792), argues that women, as rational beings, are entitled to the same education and moral standing as men.

Since women share with men the rational nature on which moral agency and civic participation depend, any system of education or law that systematically restricts women on the basis of sex alone is unjust.

Kenneth Arrow, 'Social Choice and Individual Values' (Cowles Foundation Monograph 12, Wiley, 1951), proved that no social welfare function can simultaneously satisfy unrestricted domain, non-dictatorship, Pareto efficiency, and independence of irrelevant alternatives when there are at least three alternatives.
No voting rule over three or more alternatives can jointly satisfy unrestricted domain, non-dictatorship, the Pareto criterion, and independence of irrelevant alternatives.

Fama and French, 'Common risk factors in the returns on stocks and bonds', Journal of Financial Economics 33 (1993) 3-56, introduced the three-factor model augmenting the market factor with size (SMB) and value (HML) factors.

Cross-sectional variation in average stock returns is captured reasonably well by three common risk factors: the market excess return, a small-minus-big size factor, and a high-minus-low book-to-market factor.

Reinhart and Rogoff, 'Growth in a Time of Debt', American Economic Review 100 (2010) 573-578, reported that median real GDP growth falls noticeably once gross public debt exceeds roughly 90 percent of GDP, a finding later revised after spreadsheet errors were identified by Herndon, Ash, and Pollin (Cambridge Journal of Economics 2014).
Cross-country data show a negative correlation between very high public debt-to-GDP ratios and subsequent real growth, though the strength and threshold of this relationship remain contested.

Card and Krueger, 'Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania', American Economic Review 84 (1994) 772-793, found no evidence that the 1992 New Jersey minimum wage increase reduced fast-food employment relative to Pennsylvania.
A natural experiment comparing fast-food employment in New Jersey and Pennsylvania around a minimum wage increase found no meaningful employment reduction in the treated state.

Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson, 'The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation', American Economic Review 91 (2001) 1369-1401, used settler mortality as an instrument to identify a large causal effect of institutions on long-run per-capita income.
Differences in long-run income across former colonies are largely explained by differences in early extractive versus inclusive institutions, rather than by geography alone.

Kahneman and Tversky, 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk', Econometrica 47 (1979) 263-291, documented loss aversion and a value function concave in gains and convex in losses, contrary to expected utility.
People evaluate risky prospects relative to a reference point and treat losses as roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains are pleasurable.

Jacob Mincer, 'Schooling, Experience, and Earnings' (NBER, 1974), estimated log-earnings as a linear function of years of schooling and a quadratic in experience, the specification now known as the Mincer equation.

Log hourly earnings are approximately linear in years of schooling and concave in potential labour market experience, with each additional year of schooling typically associated with about an eight to ten percent earnings premium.

Robert Solow, 'A Contribution to the Theory of Economic Growth', Quarterly Journal of Economics 70 (1956) 65-94, introduced the neoclassical one-sector growth model with diminishing returns to capital and exogenous technical progress.

In a one-sector neoclassical growth model with diminishing returns to capital, long-run growth in output per worker is driven by exogenous technological progress rather than by capital accumulation alone.

Robert E. Lucas Jr., 'Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique', Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy 1 (1976) 19-46, argued that reduced-form parameters estimated under one policy regime are generally not invariant to policy changes.
Econometric models whose coefficients are not derived from agents' structural optimization problems will generally mislead policy evaluation because agents adjust expectations when policy changes.

Black and Scholes, 'The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities', Journal of Political Economy 81 (1973) 637-654, derived the closed-form price of a European option under geometric Brownian motion and no arbitrage.

Under geometric Brownian motion for the underlying asset and a constant risk-free rate, the no-arbitrage price of a European call option admits a closed-form solution involving the cumulative standard normal distribution.

Modigliani and Miller, 'The Cost of Capital, Corporation Finance and the Theory of Investment', American Economic Review 48 (1958) 261-297, showed that in frictionless markets firm value is invariant to capital structure.
In a world without taxes, bankruptcy costs, or information asymmetries, the total value of a firm is independent of how that firm is financed through debt or equity.
John Nash, 'Equilibrium Points in N-Person Games', PNAS 36 (1950) 48-49, proved existence of mixed-strategy equilibria in every finite n-player non-cooperative game.

Every finite non-cooperative game with a finite number of players and strategies admits at least one equilibrium in which no player can benefit by unilaterally deviating, possibly in mixed strategies.

George Akerlof, 'The Market for Lemons: Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism', Quarterly Journal of Economics 84 (1970) 488-500, showed that asymmetric information about quality can cause adverse selection and market unraveling.
When sellers know product quality but buyers do not, adverse selection can drive high-quality goods out of the market even when mutually beneficial trades exist.
Michael Spence, 'Job Market Signaling', Quarterly Journal of Economics 87 (1973) 355-374, formalized education as a signal of innate productivity in a labour market with asymmetric information.
Costly education can serve as a signal of underlying worker productivity in labour markets with asymmetric information, even when schooling itself adds no human capital.

Diamond and Dybvig, 'Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity', Journal of Political Economy 91 (1983) 401-419, modeled banks as providing maturity transformation with multiple equilibria, one of which is a self-fulfilling run.
Demand-deposit banks that transform illiquid long-term assets into liquid liabilities are vulnerable to self-fulfilling runs, which deposit insurance can eliminate by ruling out the bad equilibrium.

William Vickrey, 'Counterspeculation, Auctions, and Competitive Sealed Tenders', Journal of Finance 16 (1961) 8-37, showed that the sealed-bid second-price auction has truthful bidding as a dominant strategy.
In a sealed-bid second-price auction with private values, bidding one's true valuation is a weakly dominant strategy.

Gale and Shapley, 'College Admissions and the Stability of Marriage', American Mathematical Monthly 69 (1962) 9-15, introduced the deferred acceptance algorithm producing a stable matching in two-sided markets.
The deferred acceptance algorithm always produces a stable matching in a two-sided market with strict preferences, and the outcome is optimal for the proposing side.

James Heckman, 'Sample Selection Bias as a Specification Error', Econometrica 47 (1979) 153-161, proposed a two-step estimator correcting for non-random sample selection using the inverse Mills ratio.

Ordinary least squares regression on a non-randomly selected sample produces biased estimates unless the selection process is modeled explicitly, for example by including a correction term constructed from a first-stage probit.

Imbens and Angrist, 'Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects', Econometrica 62 (1994) 467-475, showed that an instrumental variable identifies the local average treatment effect for compliers under monotonicity.

Under monotonicity, an instrumental variables estimator recovers the average treatment effect for those subjects whose treatment status is shifted by the instrument, rather than for the full population.

Dickey and Fuller, 'Distribution of the Estimators for Autoregressive Time Series With a Unit Root', Journal of the American Statistical Association 74 (1979) 427-431, derived the non-standard limiting distribution of the t-statistic for the unit-root null.
The t-statistic for testing a unit root in an autoregressive process does not follow a standard normal distribution under the null, so tabulated non-standard critical values must be used.

Robert Engle, 'Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity with Estimates of the Variance of United Kingdom Inflation', Econometrica 50 (1982) 987-1007, introduced the ARCH family of models for time-varying conditional variances.
The conditional variance of many financial and macroeconomic time series is itself time-varying and can be modeled as a function of past squared innovations.

Engle and Granger, 'Co-Integration and Error Correction: Representation, Estimation, and Testing', Econometrica 55 (1987) 251-276, established the equivalence between cointegrated systems and error-correction representations.
When two non-stationary time series share a common stochastic trend, their deviations from that trend are stationary and can be represented as an error-correction mechanism.

Mortensen and Pissarides, 'Job Creation and Job Destruction in the Theory of Unemployment', Review of Economic Studies 61 (1994) 397-415, developed the canonical search-and-matching model of equilibrium unemployment.
Equilibrium unemployment arises naturally from a search and matching friction in which vacancies and unemployed workers meet through a stochastic matching function.

John B. Taylor, 'Discretion versus policy rules in practice', Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy 39 (1993) 195-214, proposed a simple rule setting the federal funds rate as a function of inflation and the output gap.

A simple monetary policy rule that moves the short-term nominal interest rate more than one-for-one with inflation and in the same direction as the output gap tracks historical Federal Reserve behaviour reasonably well.

Milton Friedman, 'A Theory of the Consumption Function' (NBER, Princeton University Press, 1957), formulated the permanent income hypothesis, whereby consumption depends on expected long-run income rather than current income.
Households smooth consumption against transitory income fluctuations, so consumption responds much more strongly to changes in perceived permanent income than to transitory shocks.
Lucas and Prescott, 'Investment Under Uncertainty', Econometrica 39 (1971) 659-681, solved a dynamic rational-expectations equilibrium model of industry investment under stochastic demand.
In a rational-expectations competitive equilibrium, firms' investment decisions are consistent with the equilibrium stochastic process they generate for prices.

Piketty and Saez, 'Income Inequality in the United States, 1913-1998', Quarterly Journal of Economics 118 (2003) 1-39, reconstructed the long-run share of income accruing to the top one percent from US tax return data.

The share of total US pre-tax income going to the top one percent of earners fell sharply from the 1930s through the 1970s and then rose again from the 1980s onwards, approaching pre-Depression levels.

Chetty, Hendren, Kline, and Saez, 'Where is the Land of Opportunity? The Geography of Intergenerational Mobility in the United States', Quarterly Journal of Economics 129 (2014) 1553-1623, used de-identified tax records covering tens of millions of children to map intergenerational mobility across US commuting zones.

Intergenerational income mobility in the United States varies substantially across regions, with some metropolitan areas exhibiting mobility rates comparable to the most mobile European countries and others much lower.

Banerjee, Duflo, Glennerster, and Kinnan, 'The Miracle of Microfinance? Evidence from a Randomized Evaluation', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 7 (2015) 22-53, reported modest impacts of microcredit access in Hyderabad.
Randomized evaluations of microcredit in low-income urban settings have generally found modest effects on business creation and no transformative effects on household consumption or welfare.

Elinor Ostrom, 'Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action' (Cambridge University Press, 1990), documented eight design principles under which communities successfully self-govern common-pool resources.

Common-pool resources such as fisheries, forests, and irrigation systems can be sustainably managed by user communities themselves when institutions satisfy design principles such as clear boundaries, graduated sanctions, and collective-choice arrangements.

William Nordhaus, 'An Optimal Transition Path for Controlling Greenhouse Gases', Science 258 (1992) 1315-1319, introduced the DICE integrated assessment model coupling a Ramsey growth model with a climate module.

An integrated assessment model that couples a neoclassical growth framework with a simple carbon-cycle and temperature module can be used to compute optimal paths of emissions abatement and a social cost of carbon.

Martin Weitzman, 'On Modeling and Interpreting the Economics of Catastrophic Climate Change', Review of Economics and Statistics 91 (2009) 1-19, argued that fat-tailed uncertainty about climate sensitivity can dominate standard cost-benefit analysis.

Standard cost-benefit analysis of climate policy can give misleading results when the distribution of possible climate damages has a sufficiently fat right tail, because expected marginal utility losses can be unbounded.

Paul Krugman, 'Increasing Returns, Monopolistic Competition, and International Trade', Journal of International Economics 9 (1979) 469-479, developed a model of intra-industry trade driven by love-of-variety and increasing returns.

Trade between similar countries in similar products can be explained by consumer preferences for variety combined with firm-level increasing returns to scale, even in the absence of comparative advantage.

Marc Melitz, 'The Impact of Trade on Intra-Industry Reallocations and Aggregate Industry Productivity', Econometrica 71 (2003) 1695-1725, introduced firm heterogeneity into trade theory, with only the most productive firms exporting.
Trade liberalization reallocates market share toward the most productive firms within an industry, raising aggregate industry productivity through selection into exporting.

Autor, Dorn, and Hanson, 'The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States', American Economic Review 103 (2013) 2121-2168, estimated the impact of rising Chinese import competition on US commuting zones.

Rising import competition from China between 1990 and 2007 caused significant and persistent declines in manufacturing employment, wages, and labour force participation in the most exposed US local labour markets.

Charles Tiebout, 'A Pure Theory of Local Expenditures', Journal of Political Economy 64 (1956) 416-424, argued that mobile households reveal their preferences for local public goods by sorting across jurisdictions.

When households can freely move across jurisdictions offering different bundles of local public goods and taxes, their location choices can efficiently reveal preferences and support an efficient provision of those goods.

Feldstein and Horioka, 'Domestic Saving and International Capital Flows', Economic Journal 90 (1980) 314-329, documented a high correlation between national saving and domestic investment rates among OECD economies.
Despite apparent international capital mobility, national saving rates and domestic investment rates are strongly correlated across advanced economies.

Bernanke, Gertler, and Gilchrist, 'The Financial Accelerator in a Quantitative Business Cycle Framework', in Handbook of Macroeconomics Vol. 1C (Elsevier, 1999) 1341-1393, embedded costly external finance in a DSGE model.
Balance-sheet frictions that make external finance more costly than internal funds amplify and propagate shocks through the business cycle.

Robert Shiller, 'Do Stock Prices Move Too Much to be Justified by Subsequent Changes in Dividends?', American Economic Review 71 (1981) 421-436, showed that stock price volatility far exceeds that implied by the present-value model with constant discount rates.
Aggregate US stock prices have historically been far more volatile than the ex-post present value of dividends, challenging simple constant-discount-rate efficient markets models.

Mehra and Prescott, 'The Equity Premium: A Puzzle', Journal of Monetary Economics 15 (1985) 145-161, showed that the historical US equity premium is far larger than a representative-agent consumption-CAPM with plausible risk aversion can justify.

The historical excess return of equities over safe bonds in the US is much larger than can be rationalized by a representative-agent consumption-based asset pricing model with conventional levels of risk aversion.
Klemperer, 'Markets with Consumer Switching Costs', Quarterly Journal of Economics 102 (1987) 375-394, analyzed how switching costs soften price competition and can raise equilibrium prices.

When consumers face costs of switching between suppliers, firms effectively compete for future market share by pricing low initially and then exploiting locked-in customers, leading to higher average prices than under frictionless competition.

Bresnahan and Reiss, 'Entry and Competition in Concentrated Markets', Journal of Political Economy 99 (1991) 977-1009, estimated how the market size required to support each additional firm grows less than proportionally, indicating rapid convergence to competitive conduct.

In small local markets, the population required to support each additional entrant rises sharply from monopoly to duopoly but flattens quickly, suggesting that competitive conduct is approached with only a handful of firms.

Roth, Sonmez, and Unver, 'Kidney Exchange', Quarterly Journal of Economics 119 (2004) 457-488, designed matching mechanisms for paired kidney donation that are strategy-proof and produce Pareto-efficient outcomes.
Paired kidney exchange programs can be organized through strategy-proof mechanisms that increase the number of feasible transplants relative to direct donation alone.

Grossman and Hart, 'The Costs and Benefits of Ownership: A Theory of Vertical and Lateral Integration', Journal of Political Economy 94 (1986) 691-719, introduced the property-rights theory of the firm based on residual control rights over assets.
The boundaries of the firm are determined by who holds residual control rights over assets when contracts are incomplete, because ownership affects ex ante investment incentives.

Gary Becker, 'Human Capital: A Theoretical and Empirical Analysis, with Special Reference to Education' (NBER, Columbia University Press, 1964), formalized investment in schooling and training as analogous to investment in physical capital.
Schooling, training, and health can be modeled as investments that raise an individual's productivity and lifetime earnings, with returns that can be compared to those on physical capital.

Michael Grossman, 'On the Concept of Health Capital and the Demand for Health', Journal of Political Economy 80 (1972) 223-255, modeled health as a durable capital stock that depreciates with age and can be augmented by investment.
Individuals can be viewed as choosing a path of investment in health as a durable stock that yields utility directly and indirectly by expanding time available for work and leisure.

Finkelstein et al., 'The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment: Evidence from the First Year', Quarterly Journal of Economics 127 (2012) 1057-1106, used the 2008 Oregon Medicaid lottery to identify causal effects of insurance coverage.

Randomized access to Medicaid in Oregon increased healthcare utilization, reduced financial strain, and improved self-reported health, without detectable short-run effects on objective measures such as blood pressure or cholesterol.

Romer and Romer, 'A New Measure of Monetary Shocks: Derivation and Implications', NBER Working Paper 9866 (2003, later published in American Economic Review 94, 2004, 1055-1084), constructed narrative-based monetary shocks from FOMC records.

Monetary policy shocks constructed from narrative records of Federal Open Market Committee intentions produce larger and more persistent estimated effects on output and prices than shocks identified from simple reduced-form VARs.

The IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2019, Chapter 4 'The Rise of Corporate Market Power and Its Macroeconomic Effects', documented a broad-based rise in firm-level markups across advanced economies since 2000.
Firm-level markups over marginal cost have risen broadly across advanced economies since around 2000, with the increase concentrated among already-high-markup firms.

David Laibson, 'Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting', Quarterly Journal of Economics 112 (1997) 443-478, introduced quasi-hyperbolic discounting into intertemporal consumption choice and analyzed commitment devices.
People tend to discount the near future more steeply than the distant future, creating time-inconsistent preferences that can generate demand for illiquid savings vehicles as commitment devices.
Clement Greenberg, 'Avant-Garde and Kitsch', Partisan Review 6 (1939) 34-49, argued that the historical avant-garde arose as a defence of high culture against the industrial production of kitsch.
The twentieth-century avant-garde can be read as a response to the rise of industrially produced mass culture, with modernist art attempting to preserve the autonomy of aesthetic experience.
Roland Barthes, Mythologies (Seuil, 1957), analyzed everyday bourgeois culture — wrestling, steak and chips, the new Citroen — as a second-order semiological system that naturalizes ideology.
Everyday cultural objects and spectacles can operate as myths in a semiotic sense, encoding ideological meanings that their users experience as natural and self-evident.

Northrop Frye, Anatomy of Criticism (Princeton University Press, 1957), proposed a systematic theory of modes, symbols, myths, and genres, arguing that literary criticism could be a coherent conceptual discipline.

Works of literature can be classified within a structured system of modes and archetypes, allowing criticism to function as a coherent theoretical discipline rather than a series of isolated judgements.

Charles Rosen, The Classical Style: Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven (Norton, 1971), argued that the late eighteenth-century classical style was defined by the dramatic articulation of tonal areas through sonata form.

The late eighteenth-century classical style of Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven is characterized by the dramatic articulation of tonal regions, with sonata form organizing large-scale harmonic tension and resolution.

David Bordwell, Narration in the Fiction Film (University of Wisconsin Press, 1985), developed a constructivist theory of narration, distinguishing classical, art-cinema, historical-materialist, and parametric modes.
Narrative cinema can be analyzed as a set of distinct modes of narration — classical Hollywood, European art cinema, Soviet historical-materialist, and parametric — each with its own stylistic norms.

Erich Auerbach, Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (Princeton University Press, 1953; German original 1946), traced the changing representation of reality from Homer and the Hebrew Bible to Woolf.
The depiction of everyday reality in Western literature undergoes major shifts across history, from the external clarity of Homer to the fragmented interiority of twentieth-century modernist prose.

Rosalind Krauss, 'Grids', October 9 (1979) 50-64, argued that the grid functions as both a spatial and a mythic emblem of modernist art's ambition to be simultaneously anti-natural and self-contained.
The grid is a recurring formal device in modernist visual art because it enacts the ambition of autonomy from nature while insisting on flatness and self-reference.

Erwin Panofsky, Studies in Iconology (Oxford University Press, 1939), distinguished pre-iconographic description, iconographic analysis, and iconological interpretation as three levels of meaning in visual art.
The interpretation of a painting can be organized into three levels: identifying what is depicted, recognizing conventional themes, and uncovering the broader cultural meanings the image expresses.

John Berger, Ways of Seeing (BBC / Penguin, 1972), argued that oil painting as a genre is structured to celebrate private property and that the female nude is typically constructed for a male spectator.

Traditional European oil painting often frames its subjects in relation to ownership, and the female nude in particular is composed to address an implied male viewer rather than the depicted woman's own experience.

Walter Benjamin, 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1935; Zeitschrift fuer Sozialforschung V, 1936), argued that photographic and cinematic reproduction destroys the aura of the original artwork.
The reproduction of artworks through photography and film erodes the unique presence, or aura, that a single original object holds within a specific tradition and location.
Edward Said, Orientalism (Pantheon, 1978), argued that European scholarly and literary representations of the Middle East constituted a discourse that both enabled and legitimated imperial rule.
European scholarly, literary, and artistic representations of the Middle East historically formed a coherent discourse that supported and justified colonial domination of those regions.
